Disclosure alone does not limit reach or monetization; repeated non-disclosure can mean removal or YPP suspension.
facts.source_title: Disclosing use of altered or synthetic content - YouTube Help

facts.statement: FCC Declaratory Ruling FCC 24-17 (CG Docket 23-362, adopted 2 Feb, released 8 Feb 2024): the TCPA's limits on 'artificial or prerecorded voice' cover AI technologies that generate human voices, including voice cloning. Calls using AI voices need the called party's prior express consent unless an emergency purpose or exemption applies. Never let an AI voice agent make outbound sales calls without documented consent.
facts.source_title: FCC Declaratory Ruling FCC 24-17: Implications of AI Technologies on Protecting Consumers from Unwanted Robocalls and Robotexts

facts.statement: Google's Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy (last modified 17 Dec 2024) bars scams and fraud and deceptive actions; impersonating a person without disclosure in order to deceive; misleading claims of expertise in sensitive fields such as health, finance, government services and law; presenting AI-generated content as solely human-made in order to deceive; and spam, phishing and malware. Exceptions may apply for educational, documentary, scientific or artistic purposes or where substantial public benefits outweigh harms. Applies to Gemini and other Google generative AI used for marketing.
facts.source_title: Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy

facts.statement: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM05 Improper Output Handling, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM09 Misinformation, LLM10 Unbounded Consumption. Use it as the checklist for every agent that reads web pages, emails or reviews, holds API keys, or can publish or spend.
facts.source_title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025

facts.statement: OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection: direct injection comes from user input; indirect injection comes from external content (websites, files) that the model processes. OWASP says no foolproof prevention is known, only layered mitigation: constrain the model's role, validate output formats with deterministic code, filter inputs and outputs, enforce least privilege, require human approval for high-risk actions, segregate and mark untrusted external content, and run regular adversarial testing.
facts.source_title: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection

facts.statement: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 was released 26 Jan 2023 with four core functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage); the Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1, was released 26 Jul 2024 with risks and actions specific to generative AI. NIST says AI RMF 1.0 is being revised under the White House AI Action Plan, and on 7 Apr 2026 it released a concept note for a critical-infrastructure profile. Map agent evaluations and red-team results to these functions in the self-evolution loop.
facts.source_title: AI Risk Management Framework - NIST

facts.statement: Google's guidance on generative AI content: AI can help research and structure original content, but content must meet Search Essentials and spam policies; generating many pages without adding value may be scaled content abuse. Manually fact-check and review all AI output before publishing, including titles, meta descriptions, structured data and image alt text, because models can be wrong. Consider telling readers how automation was used. Quality rater ratings do not directly influence ranking.
facts.source_title: Google Search's guidance on using generative AI content on your website

facts.statement: Google Merchant Center requires AI-generated product images to carry IPTC DigitalSourceType metadata, normally TrainedAlgorithmicMedia (also CompositeSynthetic or AlgorithmicMedia), and the tag must not be stripped, including from Product Studio images. AI-written product titles and descriptions go in structured_title and structured_description with digital_source_type 'trained_algorithmic_media' and the text in content, instead of or alongside title and description.
facts.source_title: Merchant Center - AI-generated content requirements

facts.statement: Google (8 Feb 2023): appropriate use of AI or automation is not against its guidelines; its systems reward original, high-quality content with E-E-A-T however it is produced, while automation used mainly to manipulate rankings is spam. Add accurate bylines where readers would ask 'Who wrote this?' and AI disclosures where they would ask 'How was this created?'. Google says listing AI as the author is probably not the best way to show AI was involved.
facts.source_title: Google Search's guidance about AI-generated content

facts.statement: Google's 'helpful, people-first content' page asks Who, How and Why. Who: show clear bylines linking to author background; fabricated authors, AI-generated headshots or false credentials are deceptive. How: explain how content was made, including automation or AI, when readers would reasonably wonder. Why: the main purpose must be helping visitors, not attracting search visits. Trust is the most important part of E-E-A-T, and YMYL topics (health, finance, safety) get extra weight.
facts.source_title: Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content

facts.statement: Google lists search-engine-first warning signs: producing many articles on varied topics to chase traffic, summarizing others without adding value, writing about trends without expertise, changing dates to seem fresh, and writing to a word count - Google says it has no preferred word count. Self-check: would you bookmark, share or recommend the page; ask trusted people unaffiliated with your site for honest feedback.
facts.source_title: Creating Helpful, Reliable, People-First Content

facts.statement: Google spam policies: scaled content abuse is generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings and not help users, for example using generative AI to make many pages without adding value, scraping feeds or search results into many pages, stitching content from other pages, creating multiple sites to hide the scale, or pages that make little sense but contain keywords. Expired domain abuse is buying an expired domain and repurposing it mainly to manipulate rankings, such as affiliate content on a site formerly used by a government agency. Every programmatic page needs unique value before indexing.
facts.source_title: Spam Policies for Google Web Search

facts.statement: Search Quality Rater Guidelines (11 Sep 2025): 'Trust is the most important member of the E-E-A-T family' - untrustworthy pages have low E-E-A-T however expert they seem. Raters judge E-E-A-T from what the site and creators say about themselves (About, profile pages), what independent sources say, and what is visible on the page. Reviews by the manufacturer or by paid influencers are less trustworthy due to conflict of interest. Customer service information counts toward trust for online stores.
facts.source_title: Search Quality Rater Guidelines (September 11, 2025)

facts.statement: Search Quality Rater Guidelines (Sep 2025): pages made at scale with no original content or added value are rated Lowest no matter how they are created, including automated tools (generative AI or otherwise), scraped feeds with synonymizing or translating, and stitched content; raters use Lowest when they strongly suspect scaled abuse even if unsure AI was used. Lowest also applies when all or almost all main content is copied, paraphrased, embedded, or auto or AI generated with little effort, originality or added value, even with credit to the source.
facts.source_title: Search Quality Rater Guidelines (September 11, 2025)

facts.statement: Google Article structured data has no required properties. Mark up every author shown on the page as a separate author entry, typed Person or Organization, with url or sameAs to a page about them; author.name holds only the name, with job titles, honorifics and publisher in their own properties. Use ISO 8601 datePublished and dateModified with a timezone (otherwise Googlebot's timezone is used). Provide images in 16x9, 4x3 and 1x1 ratios of at least 50,000 pixels (width times height) each.
facts.source_title: Article (Article, NewsArticle, BlogPosting) structured data

facts.statement: Google's guidance on page dates: show a prominent visible date labeled 'Published' or 'Last updated', add datePublished and/or dateModified in Article, BlogPosting or other CreativeWork markup, keep visible and structured dates consistent, add a timezone if you include a time, never use future dates or the dates of events the page describes, and remove other confusing dates if Google picks the wrong one.
facts.source_title: Influencing your byline dates in Google Search

facts.statement: Altay and Gilardi (PNAS Nexus, 2024; two preregistered experiments, N=4,976, US and UK): labeling headlines 'AI-generated' lowered perceived accuracy and sharing intent for true and false headlines alike, and for human-made headlines wrongly labeled AI. In Study 1 the label cut accuracy ratings by about 2.66 points, roughly a third of a 'False' label's effect. The penalty came from assuming AI wrote everything; describing AI as polishing a human draft removed it. Word AI disclosures to state the human role precisely.
facts.source_title: People are skeptical of headlines labeled as AI-generated, even if true or human-made, because they assume full AI automation

facts.statement: Aggarwal et al., 'GEO: Generative Engine Optimization' (KDD 2024): on GEO-bench, adding quotations raised position-adjusted word-count visibility about 43% (27.8 vs 19.5 baseline), adding statistics about 33%, citing sources about 28%, while keyword stuffing lowered it about 9%. Gains were largest for lower-ranked sources (citing sources: +115% at rank 5, -30% at rank 1). The abstract says GEO can boost visibility by up to 40%. Results on Perplexity.ai differed from GEO-bench, with keyword stuffing again lowering visibility; check the paper's tables before quoting Perplexity numbers. Add sourced quotes and statistics to pages you want AI engines to cite.
facts.source_title: GEO: Generative Engine Optimization

facts.statement: EU Price Indication Directive Art. 6a (added by Omnibus Directive 2019/2161, applied from 28 May 2022): any announced price reduction must show the prior price, meaning the lowest price the trader applied in a period of at least 30 days before the reduction. Member States may set different rules for goods that deteriorate or expire quickly, a shorter period for products on sale under 30 days, and, for progressively increased reductions, use the price before the first reduction. Check the national transposition for each market.
facts.source_title: Directive (EU) 2019/2161 (Omnibus Directive)

facts.statement: CJEU, Case C-330/23 Aldi Sud (26 Sep 2024): a price reduction announced as a percentage, or as a promotional claim stressing an advantageous price such as 'price highlight', must be calculated on the basis of the lowest price the trader applied in the 30 days before the reduction. Merely showing that lowest price for information is not enough.
facts.source_title: CJEU Press Release No 152/24 - Judgment in Case C-330/23 Aldi Sud

facts.statement: Directive (EU) 2023/2673 adds Article 11a to the Consumer Rights Directive, applied from 19 Jun 2026: for distance contracts concluded online, traders must offer a withdrawal function labeled 'withdraw from contract here' or an unambiguous equivalent, continuously available during the withdrawal period, prominent and easy to reach. It lets the consumer send an online withdrawal statement with name, contract details and the channel for confirmation, which the trader must confirm on a durable medium. Add it to every EU checkout and account area.
facts.source_title: Directive (EU) 2023/2673

facts.statement: The FTC Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees (announced 17 Dec 2024, effective 12 May 2025) covers only live-event tickets and short-term lodging. Covered businesses must clearly show the total price including all mandatory fees whenever they show a price, make that total more prominent than other pricing, and not misrepresent any fee. Taxes and shipping may be excluded but must be disclosed before payment. Other industries face case-by-case FTC Act enforcement, so show all-in prices anyway.
facts.source_title: Federal Trade Commission Announces Bipartisan Rule Banning Junk Ticket and Hotel Fees

facts.statement: FTC click-to-cancel status: the Eighth Circuit vacated the FTC's 2024 Negative Option Rule amendments on 8 Jul 2025 (Custom Communications v. FTC). On 11 Mar 2026 the FTC announced an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on negative option marketing (published in the Federal Register on 13 Mar 2026), asking whether to amend the rule and referring to the vacated 2024 rule as one option. No federal click-to-cancel rule is in force; ROSCA, the FTC Act and state laws still apply.
facts.source_title: FTC Seeks Public Comment in Response to Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking Regarding Negative Option Marketing Practices

facts.statement: FTC v. Amazon (settled 25 Sep 2025): Amazon agreed to a USD 1 billion civil penalty and USD 1.5 billion in consumer redress for about 35 million consumers over unwanted Prime enrollment and hard-to-use cancellation (FTC Act and ROSCA). It must show a clearly visible option to decline Prime, clearly disclose key terms during enrollment, and let people cancel using the same method they used to sign up; a third-party supervisor monitors the refunds.
facts.source_title: FTC Secures Historic $2.5 Billion Settlement Against Amazon

facts.statement: UK DMCC Act unfair commercial practices rules apply from April 2025 (6 Apr 2025): drip pricing is banned and invitations to purchase must show the total price including mandatory fees. On 15 Apr 2026 the CMA fined the AA GBP 4.2 million (after a 40% settlement discount from GBP 7 million) for a mandatory GBP 3 booking fee left out of the upfront price; fines can reach 10% of global turnover (or GBP 300,000 if higher). CMA guidance on pricing (CMA209) covers drip and partitioned pricing.
facts.source_title: CMA orders the AA and BSM driving schools to refund learner drivers over drip pricing

facts.statement: UK subscription contracts regime (DMCC Act Part 4 Ch 2): draft government guidance published in Oct 2026 (reported as 19 Oct 2026) says the rules apply to subscription contracts entered into on or after 1 January 2027, but the accompanying draft Consumer Subscription Contracts (Cancellation and Information) Regulations 2026 still need Parliament's approval, so the date is not yet confirmed. Under the regime traders must give key pre-contract information, send reminder notices before renewals and after free or discounted trials, allow a 14-day cooling-off period, and let online sign-ups end the contract online in a straightforward way.
facts.source_title: Draft Guidance on Consumer Subscription Contracts (DMCCA Part 4 Chapter 2)

facts.statement: California's amended Automatic Renewal Law (AB 2863), for contracts entered, amended or extended from 1 Jul 2025, requires express affirmative consent to auto-renewal terms, online cancellation for online sign-ups without steps that obstruct or delay it, an annual reminder through the enrollment channel stating product, charge amount and frequency and how to cancel, notice 3-21 days before free or discounted trials over 31 days end, and notice 7-30 days before an accepted price increase.
facts.source_title: Attorney General Bonta Issues Consumer Alert on California's Automatic Renewal Law

facts.statement: Thomas and Morwitz (Journal of Consumer Research, 2005, 32(1):54-64): nine-ending prices such as 2.99 are perceived as smaller than a price one cent higher only when the leftmost digit changes (2.99 vs 3.00, not 2.89 vs 2.90). The effect is stronger when the comparison price is close and also appears with other multi-digit numbers. Use charm endings where they drop the left digit; elsewhere they add little.
facts.source_title: Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition

facts.statement: Anderson and Simester (Quantitative Marketing and Economics, 2003, 1(1):93-110) ran three field experiments in a mail-order catalog varying price endings: a 9 ending increased demand in all three. The lift was larger for new items than for items sold in earlier years, and there is some evidence that 9 endings work less well when 'Sale' cues are also used. 9 endings likely help most when buyers have little price information, such as new products or launches.
facts.source_title: Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments

facts.statement: Lacetera, Pope and Sydnor (American Economic Review, 2012, 102(5):2206-36), using more than 22 million wholesale used-car sales, found left-digit bias: prices drop sharply when odometer readings cross 10,000-mile thresholds, with smaller drops at 1,000-mile thresholds, driven mainly by final consumers. It is large-scale field evidence that buyers anchor on leftmost digits, which supports keeping displayed prices just under a round threshold.
facts.source_title: Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market

facts.statement: Ariely, Loewenstein and Prelec (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2003, 118(1):73-106), six experiments: initial valuations of familiar products and experiences were strongly influenced by arbitrary anchors, sometimes the last digits of a person's social security number, while later valuations stayed consistent relative to that first anchor. The first price a buyer sees shapes willingness to pay, so show the reference plan or price first, and keep any anchor truthful under EU and UK price rules.
facts.source_title: 'Coherent Arbitrariness': Stable Demand Curves Without Stable Preferences

facts.statement: Huber, Payne and Puto (Journal of Consumer Research, 1982, 9(1):90-98): adding an asymmetrically dominated option - one beaten by the target but not by the competitor - can raise the target's choice share, violating the regularity assumption of standard choice models (the decoy effect). In pricing pages, a plan clearly worse than the one you want chosen can lift that plan; test it rather than assume, and never invent a fake plan or price.
facts.source_title: Adding Asymmetrically Dominated Alternatives: Violations of Regularity and the Similarity Hypothesis

facts.statement: OpenAI's ChatGPT plugin guidelines (the app directory became the Plugin directory on 9 Jul 2026, per OpenAI's help center): plugins may currently sell only physical goods; digital products or services (subscriptions, digital content, tokens, credits) are not allowed, directly or indirectly (e.g. freemium upsells). Plugins may link to an informational plans page but not directly to checkout; purchases happen on your own domain. Instant Checkout is in beta for select marketplace partners only.
facts.source_title: OpenAI plugin guidelines

facts.statement: OpenAI plugin guidelines: plugins must not serve advertisements, must not add ChatGPT-specific fees or surcharges, and must not offer a worse version than your own site.
facts.source_title: OpenAI plugin guidelines

facts.statement: OpenAI plugin review rules for tools: tool names must be unique within your MCP server, ideally a verb for the real action, without misleading, promotional or comparative words like 'best' or 'official'; descriptions must not manipulate how the model selects or uses other plugins; every tool needs explicit boolean readOnlyHint, destructiveHint and openWorldHint values.
facts.source_title: OpenAI plugin guidelines

facts.statement: OpenAI plugin data and audience rules: collect minimum data; do not request full conversation history or precise location; protected health information is restricted. Plugins must suit general audiences including users aged 13-17 and must not target children under 13; submissions come from verified individuals or organizations, and authenticated plugins must supply a full-featured demo login.
facts.source_title: OpenAI plugin guidelines

facts.statement: Anthropic's Usage Policy version effective 12 Nov 2026 prohibits impersonating real people or entities or creating fake personas, and lists fake reviews, sockpuppets and astroturfing as deceptive artificial activity; clearly disclosed parody, satire or fiction is allowed.
facts.source_title: Anthropic Usage Policy

facts.statement: Anthropic's Usage Policy effective 12 Nov 2026: consumer-facing chatbots and agents must disclose that users are interacting with AI rather than a human, at the start of each session or in the interface; political content must not be false or misleading, and mass automated messages to voters must not conceal their artificial origin; high-risk AI recommendations (legal, medical, finance, credit, employment, housing) need meaningful review by a qualified person.
facts.source_title: Anthropic Usage Policy

facts.statement: Gartner 2026 CMO Spend Survey: marketing budgets average 7.8% of company revenue in 2026, up from 7.7% in 2025 (effectively flat). 56% of CMOs say they lack the budget for their 2026 strategy and 54% report insufficient resources. Sample: 401 CMOs/marketing leaders in North America, UK and Europe, fielded Jan-Mar 2026, mostly firms with revenue over $1B. Use as a large-enterprise reference when sizing a marketing budget; not a target for startups or SMBs.
facts.source_title: Gartner 2026 CMO Spend Survey press release

facts.statement: Gartner 2026 CMO Spend Survey: CMOs allocate on average 15.3% of marketing budgets to AI initiatives. 70% call becoming an AI leader a critical 2026 goal, but only 30% report mature AI readiness and 70% say their processes are not mature enough to scale AI. AI-ready organizations put 21.3% of budget into AI and run budgets of 8.9% of revenue vs the 7.8% average. Use to benchmark AI spend share for large firms (n=401, mostly >$1B revenue); correlation only, not proof that AI spend raises budgets.
facts.source_title: Gartner 2026 CMO Spend Survey press release

facts.statement: Gartner 2025 CMO Spend Survey: paid media is the largest budget line at 30.6% of marketing budgets (2.4% of company revenue); budgets stayed at 7.7% of revenue in 2024 and 2025, and 59% of CMOs reported insufficient budget. Sample: 402 marketing leaders, NA/UK/Europe, Feb-Mar 2025, mostly >$1B revenue. Use to sanity-check the paid-media share of a large-firm plan; Gartner notes media inflation means each dollar buys less. Not a guide for small or early-stage budgets.
facts.source_title: Gartner 2025 CMO Spend Survey press release

facts.statement: Operating model, agencies vs in-house (Gartner 2025 CMO Spend Survey): 39% of CMOs planned to cut agency budgets (top moves: drop unproductive agency relationships, streamline rosters, renegotiate scopes) and 39% planned to cut labor spend (simplify overlapping roles, reduce headcount). 22% said GenAI had reduced their reliance on external agencies for creativity and strategy. Use when advising on agency roster and in-house capacity for large firms (n=402); intentions, not measured outcomes.
facts.source_title: Gartner 2025 CMO Spend Survey press release

facts.statement: Martech stack sizing (Gartner 2023 Marketing Technology Survey, 405 marketing leaders, May-Jun 2023): organizations used on average 33% of their martech stack's capabilities, down from 42% in 2022 and 58% in 2020, while technology took 25.4% of the 2023 marketing budget. Only 11% raised utilization by more than 10 points in a year; firms using over 50% of their stack were less likely to face martech cuts. Use to argue for fewer, fully adopted tools before adding new ones; the data is from 2023.
facts.source_title: Gartner Survey Finds 63% of Marketing Leaders Plan to Invest in Generative AI in the Next 24 Months

facts.statement: ANA 'The Continued Rise of the In-House Agency' (2023 edition): 82% of ANA client-side members have an in-house agency, up from 78% (2018), 58% (2013) and 42% (2008); the ANA expects penetration to peak at 85-90%. Use as evidence that in-house plus external agencies is the norm for large US advertisers, not that in-house is cheaper or better; the ANA membership skews to large brands and the summary page gives no cost or quality comparison.
facts.source_title: The Continued Rise of the In-House Agency: 2023 Edition (ANA)

facts.statement: Gartner sales survey (646 B2B buyers, Aug-Sep 2025): 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience and 45% used AI during a recent purchase. Buyers who reach high decision confidence are twice as likely to report a high-quality deal. Use to design self-serve evaluation content (pricing, proof, ROI tools) and to arm sellers for value clarity; it measures stated preference, not that rep-free deals close faster or larger.
facts.source_title: Gartner Sales Survey Finds 67% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Experience

facts.statement: 95:5 rule (John Dawes, Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, as reported by Marketing Week): only about 5% of B2B buyers are in market to buy at any given time; the other 95% will not buy for months or even years. Implication: judge B2B marketing on reach of all category buyers and brand building, not only short-term leads. Use when a B2B plan is all bottom-funnel. A rule of thumb from an industry research programme (not peer-reviewed), not a precise ratio; the share in market varies with each category's purchase cycle. The page is an undated news repost.
facts.source_title: The 95:5 rule is the new 60:40 rule (Ehrenberg-Bass Institute)

facts.statement: Brand/activation balance (Binet & Field, IPA Databank): in B2C, efficiency is typically maximised with about 60% of the communications budget on brand building and 40% on activation; in B2B the optimum is about 46% brand / 54% activation (1998-2018 B2B cases). Use as a starting split for an established brand with enough budget for both, then adjust by category, price point and brand size. Not a law: the B2B estimate rests on fewer than 50 award-entry cases skewed to the UK and large budgets.
facts.source_title: The 5 Principles of Growth in B2B Marketing (Les Binet & Peter Field, The B2B Institute at LinkedIn)

facts.statement: Excess share of voice (ESOV = share of voice minus share of market): brands that keep SOV above SOM tend to grow, those below tend to shrink. In the IPA Databank, 10 points of ESOV are associated with about +0.6 points of market share a year for consumer brands and +0.7 for B2B, all else equal (Binet & Field). Use to set budgets: pick a share target, set the SOV needed, then estimate the spend. Not for brand-new categories or when SOV cannot be measured; B2B results are tentative (small sample).
facts.source_title: The 5 Principles of Growth in B2B Marketing (Les Binet & Peter Field, The B2B Institute at LinkedIn)

facts.statement: In B2B, customer acquisition (penetration) strategies tend to be much more effective at driving growth than customer retention/loyalty strategies, matching B2C evidence (Binet & Field, B2B IPA Databank cases 1998-2018, fewer than 50 cases). A LinkedIn survey cited in the report suggests many B2B marketers nonetheless place more belief in loyalty-based strategies. Use to weight plans toward reaching new category buyers rather than only upselling existing accounts. Not an argument to neglect retention economics in subscription businesses; it concerns what drives share growth.
facts.source_title: The 5 Principles of Growth in B2B Marketing (Les Binet & Peter Field, The B2B Institute at LinkedIn)

facts.statement: Campaign objective matters (Binet & Field, IPA Databank B2B cases 1998-2018): campaigns with the objective of building brand fame deliver far more large business effects than those just building awareness. In B2B, emotional messaging is better at building brands and driving long-term sales and profit, while rational arguments and product detail work best in activation campaigns aimed at buyers most likely to buy. Use to set brand-campaign objectives and pair emotional brand work with rational activation. Small sample (fewer than 50 B2B cases) from award entries, so treat as directional.
facts.source_title: The 5 Principles of Growth in B2B Marketing (Les Binet & Peter Field, The B2B Institute at LinkedIn)

facts.statement: Creative quality multiplies media weight (System1, from Peter Field's IPA analysis): an average 2-star ad delivers about 0.5 points of market share gain per 10 points of ESOV, while a 5-star ad delivers about 3 points; only 4% of the many thousands of ads System1 tested reach 5 stars. Use to argue that pretesting and improving creative can be worth more than extra spend. Vendor-published figures from System1's own rating; no sample size or method detail on the page.
facts.source_title: The System1 Guarantee: How? What? Why? (System1)

facts.statement: Peter Field's 'The Crisis in Creative Effectiveness' (IPA, ~600 IPA Effectiveness Award cases, 1996-2018): creatively awarded campaigns had become no more effective than non-awarded ones, the lowest point in 24 years of data, with short-termism (more short-term sales activation among awarded work) named as the driver. Use when advising that creative awards are not proof of business effect and that creative should serve long-term brand goals. Award-entry data, UK-skewed.
facts.source_title: The Crisis in Creative Effectiveness (Peter Field, IPA)

facts.statement: Double jeopardy (Ehrenberg, Goodhardt & Barwise, Journal of Marketing 1990): in any period a small brand has far fewer buyers than a large brand, and its buyers also buy it somewhat less often. Loyalty differences between brands mostly follow size. Use to set realistic goals: a brand grows mainly by adding buyers (penetration), so plans that promise share gains from loyalty alone are suspect. Known exceptions exist (niche and change-of-pace brands).
facts.source_title: Double Jeopardy Revisited (Journal of Marketing)

facts.statement: Brand salience / mental availability (Romaniuk & Sharp, Marketing Theory 2004): salience is the brand's propensity to be noticed or come to mind in buying situations, reflecting the quantity and quality of memory links buyers hold. It is broader than 'top of mind' first mention and distinct from awareness or attitude. Use to brief brand tracking on links to buying situations, not just unaided awareness. Not a measure of liking or preference.
facts.source_title: Conceptualizing and measuring brand salience (Marketing Theory)

facts.statement: Category entry points (CEPs, Jenni Romaniuk): the buying situations and cues that bring a category to mind, phrased as 'looking for a brand that...'. Generate them with the W's: why (motives), when (timing), where, while (co-activities), with/for whom, with what (co-purchased categories) and how feeling. Then prioritise CEPs, build them into communications and measure linkage. Use to pick which situations ads should link the brand to. Not a list of channels or places to buy.
facts.source_title: Category Entry Points in a B2B World (Jenni Romaniuk, B2B Institute at LinkedIn and Ehrenberg-Bass Institute)

facts.statement: Mental availability metrics from a CEP survey (Romaniuk): Mental Market Share = brand's CEP links / all brands' CEP links; Mental Penetration = share of category buyers linking the brand to at least one CEP; Network Size = average links among those with mental penetration. Example (UK business banking, n=609): Barclays 9.8% MMS, 78% MPen, network 7.9 vs RBS 4.4%, 53%, 5.2. Use as brand-health KPIs alongside sales. Needs a survey of category buyers, not just customers.
facts.source_title: Category Entry Points in a B2B World (Jenni Romaniuk, B2B Institute at LinkedIn and Ehrenberg-Bass Institute)

facts.statement: BCG growth-share matrix (Bruce Henderson, BCG 1970): plot products by relative market share and market growth. Stars (high share, high growth) may not fund themselves; cash cows (high share, low growth) throw off surplus cash that should not be reinvested in the same product; question marks (low share, high growth) need cash and are liabilities unless they become leaders; pets (low share, low growth) are near liquidation value. Use for portfolio cash allocation across products; it ignores synergies and assumes share drives margin.
facts.source_title: The Product Portfolio (Bruce Henderson, BCG)

facts.statement: Porter's five forces (HBR, 2008 update of the 1979 article): industry profitability is shaped by rivalry among established competitors, the bargaining power of customers and of suppliers, the threat of new entrants and the threat of substitutes. Managers often define competition too narrowly as today's direct rivals. Use at market entry or category choice to find a position that is more profitable and less exposed; it describes industry structure, not how to win inside it.
facts.source_title: The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy (Michael E. Porter, HBR)

facts.statement: Porter, 'What Is Strategy?' (HBR 1996): operational effectiveness (doing the same activities better) is necessary but rivals copy it, so it rarely yields lasting advantage. Strategy means performing different activities or the same ones differently, choosing trade-offs (what not to do) and building fit so activities reinforce each other. Use to test a plan: if a competitor could copy it by adopting best practice, it is not a strategy. Not a template for tactics.
facts.source_title: What Is Strategy? (Michael E. Porter, HBR)

facts.statement: Jobs to be done (Christensen Institute): a job is the progress a person wants to make in a particular circumstance; people pull products into their lives to make that progress. Jobs have functional, social and emotional dimensions. In the milkshake case, morning buyers used a shake to stave off hunger and ease the commute, so the real competition was bananas and bagels, not other shakes. Use to define competitors by the alternatives buyers actually consider and to find switching triggers; not a substitute for demand sizing.
facts.source_title: Jobs to Be Done theory (Clayton Christensen Institute)

facts.statement: Positioning in five components (April Dunford): competitive alternatives (what customers would use if you did not exist, including doing nothing), differentiated capabilities, the value those deliver, the target customers who care most about that value, and the market category that makes the value obvious. Work them in that order. Use for B2B/tech products where buyers misunderstand what the product is. Not a messaging or tagline exercise; messaging comes after.
facts.source_title: A Quickstart Guide to Positioning (April Dunford)

facts.statement: OKRs (Objectives and Key Results), created by Andy Grove at Intel and brought to Google by John Doerr in 1999: an Objective states what to achieve and typically 3-5 Key Results measure progress. Separate committed OKRs (expected to be fully met) from aspirational stretch OKRs. Grade at cycle end (yes/no, red-yellow-green, or Google's 0.0-1.0). Use to tie marketing work to a revenue objective each quarter; not a task list.
facts.source_title: OKR meaning, definition and examples (What Matters)

facts.statement: Marketing mix modeling data rules (Meta Robyn analyst's guide): use at least two years of weekly data (4-5 years if only monthly), actual spend and impressions, digital split at least by channel, and about 10 observations per independent variable (n about 7-10x p). Model fit: R2 below 0.8 is weak, 0.8-0.9 acceptable, above 0.9 ideal. Rebuild rather than refresh when most data is new. Use to decide if a client is ready for MMM; small or new brands usually are not.
facts.source_title: Robyn: Analyst's guide to MMM (Meta open source)

facts.statement: MMM modelling practice (Meta Robyn guide): model carryover with adstock (geometric theta ranges: TV 0.3-0.8, OOH/print/radio 0.1-0.4, digital 0-0.3) and diminishing returns with a Hill saturation curve; calibrate the model with randomized experiments (conversion lift, geo tests) matched in period and metric; ridge regression handles correlated channels. The budget allocator has no accuracy guarantee. Use MMM for cross-channel allocation and validate shifts with tests; not for daily bid decisions.
facts.source_title: Robyn: Analyst's guide to MMM (Meta open source)

facts.statement: Incrementality testing in Google Ads (Conversion Lift): a test splits the audience into a treatment group that sees ads and a control group that does not, by user (user-based) or by geography (geo-based, which supports offline data); lift is the difference in conversions. User-based studies report incremental conversions, relative lift, iCPA and iROAS (iROAS only if conversion values are assigned); geo-based studies report iROAS, incremental conversions, conversion value and cost. Not available to every account (contact your Google account representative). Use to validate platform-reported ROAS before scaling a channel.
facts.source_title: About Conversion Lift (Google Ads Help)

facts.statement: Geo experiments (Vaver & Koehler, Google 2011): randomly assign non-overlapping geographic regions to treatment or control, run geo-targeted ads only in treatment, and compare outcomes to estimate ad effectiveness. Google reports the method is conceptually simple, has a systematic design process and gives easy-to-read results, including for search spend. Use when user-level holdouts are impossible (privacy limits, offline sales). Needs enough comparable regions and volume.
facts.source_title: Measuring Ad Effectiveness Using Geo Experiments (Google)

facts.statement: Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter: ask four questions (too cheap to trust quality, a bargain, getting expensive but still considered, too expensive) and plot cumulative curves; crossings give the optimal and indifference price points and the acceptable range between marginal cheapness and marginal expensiveness. Sawtooth advises using it mainly for new-to-the-world products and adding Newton-Miller-Smith purchase-intent questions; it ignores competitors and does not predict sales on its own.
facts.source_title: Van Westendorp Pricing Sensitivity Meter (Sawtooth Software)

facts.statement: Gabor-Granger pricing: show a respondent a (randomized) price and ask purchase likelihood, then step prices up or down until intent changes. Output a demand curve, a revenue curve (price x share willing to buy) and its revenue-maximizing price (profit-maximizing if costs are known). Use for new launches or repricing one product. Limits: no competitor context and no attribute trade-offs; use conjoint for those, and Van Westendorp for a price range.
facts.source_title: Gabor-Granger Pricing Method (Sawtooth Software)

facts.statement: Conjoint analysis (Green & Srinivasan, Journal of Marketing 1990, updating their 1978 review): estimate how buyers trade off product attributes, including price, from their preferences across attribute combinations; the review covers approaches for many attributes, reliability and validity checks, and choice simulators that predict share for new configurations. Use for packaging, tier design and price within a competitive set. Needs careful attribute design and an adequate sample; heavier than Van Westendorp or Gabor-Granger.
facts.source_title: Conjoint Analysis in Marketing: New Developments with Implications for Research and Practice (Journal of Marketing)

facts.statement: Customer-based brand equity (Keller, Journal of Marketing 1993): brand equity is the differential effect of brand knowledge on consumer response to the brand's marketing, compared with the same marketing for an unnamed or fictitious version. Brand knowledge = brand awareness plus brand image (associations); equity exists when the consumer is familiar with the brand and holds favorable, strong and unique associations. Use to structure brand audits and tracking; not a financial valuation method.
facts.source_title: Conceptualizing, Measuring, and Managing Customer-Based Brand Equity (Journal of Marketing)

facts.statement: Valuing customers (Gupta, Lehmann & Stuart, JMR 2004): customer value is the expected sum of discounted future earnings. Across five public firms, a 1% improvement in retention raised firm value by about 5%, versus 1% for a 1% margin improvement and 0.1% for a 1% cut in acquisition cost; a 1% retention gain had almost five times the impact of a 1% change in discount rate. Use to prioritise retention work in subscription models; based on five firms, so a direction, not a constant.
facts.source_title: Valuing Customers (Journal of Marketing Research)

facts.statement: Forecasting repeat purchases for LTV (Fader, Hardie & Lee, Marketing Science 2005): the BG/NBD model predicts future transactions from customers' past purchasing, gives results very similar to the Pareto/NBD 'counting your customers' model in a wide range of settings, and its parameters can be estimated in Excel. Use for non-contractual businesses (e-commerce, marketplaces) where churn is unobserved; for subscriptions, model observed churn directly.
facts.source_title: "Counting Your Customers" the Easy Way: An Alternative to the Pareto/NBD Model (Marketing Science)

facts.statement: Return on marketing via customer equity (Rust, Lemon & Zeithaml, Journal of Marketing 2004): trade off strategy options by projected change in customer equity (sum of current and future customers' lifetime values) relative to the incremental spend. Lifetime value comes from category purchase frequency, quantity, brand-switching patterns and contribution margin; switching can be estimated with a logit model on panel or survey data. Use to compare investments (quality, ads, loyalty) on one financial scale.
facts.source_title: Return on Marketing: Using Customer Equity to Focus Marketing Strategy (Journal of Marketing)

facts.statement: Net Promoter is not uniquely predictive (Keiningham et al., Journal of Marketing 2007): using longitudinal data from 21 firms and 15,500+ interviews in the Norwegian Customer Satisfaction Barometer, plus ACSI comparisons, the authors could not replicate claims that Net Promoter is clearly superior to other measures for predicting revenue growth in the industries cited as exemplars. Use NPS as one diagnostic, not the single growth KPI; pair it with retention and revenue metrics.
facts.source_title: A Longitudinal Examination of Net Promoter and Firm Revenue Growth (Journal of Marketing)

facts.statement: Marketing's impact on firm value (Edeling & Fischer, JMR meta-analysis of 488 elasticities from 83 studies): mean stock-market elasticity is 0.04 for advertising spend and 0.54 for marketing assets; customer-related assets (0.72) beat brand-related assets (0.33). Advertising elasticities are lower in concentrated industries, and asset elasticities are higher in recessions. Use when making the finance case: build customer and brand assets, not just spend. Elasticities vary with study design.
facts.source_title: Marketing's Impact on Firm Value: Generalizations from a Meta-Analysis (Journal of Marketing Research)

facts.statement: Spending in recessions (Srinivasan, Lilien & Sridhar, Journal of Marketing 2011; 10,000+ firm-years of US public firms, 1969-2008, seven recessions): whether raising R&D or advertising in a recession helps profits and stock returns depends on market share, financial leverage and B2B/B2C goods or services. Examples: 98% of B2C goods firms underspend on R&D and 92% of B2C services firms overspend on advertising. Use for downturn budget advice, case by case.
facts.source_title: Should Firms Spend More on Research and Development and Advertising during Recessions? (Journal of Marketing)

facts.statement: Bass diffusion model (Management Science 1969): the timing of first purchase of a new product depends on innovative and imitative behavior, with imitation tied to the number of previous buyers; tested on 11 consumer durables, it predicted the sales peak and its timing well. Use to forecast adoption curves for a new category or product once a few periods of sales exist, or by analogy to similar products. Not for repeat-purchase sales or for brands within an established category.
facts.source_title: A New Product Growth for Model Consumer Durables (Management Science)

facts.statement: Advertising elasticity meta-analysis (Sethuraman, Tellis & Briesch, JMR 2011): 751 short-term and 402 long-term brand advertising elasticities from 56 studies (1960-2008). Mean short-term elasticity is 0.12 (a 10% ad increase gives about 1.2% more sales) and long-term 0.24, both below earlier estimates, and elasticity has declined over time. It is higher for durables, early life-cycle brands, and GRP-based measures. Use for realistic ad-response assumptions; brand-level averages, not channel-specific.
facts.source_title: How Well Does Advertising Work? Generalizations from Meta-Analysis of Brand Advertising Elasticities (JMR)

facts.statement: Price elasticity meta-analysis (Bijmolt, van Heerde & Pieters, JMR 2005): across 1,851 price elasticities from 81 studies, the average is -2.62 (a 1% price cut raises sales about 2.6%). Sales elasticities have grown in magnitude over four decades; models that correct for price endogeneity give larger elasticities, while accounting for heterogeneity does not change them significantly. Use as a prior for price tests; category and brand values vary widely.
facts.source_title: New Empirical Generalizations on the Determinants of Price Elasticity (JMR)

facts.statement: TV ad ROI at scale (Shapiro, Hitsch & Tuchman, Econometrica 2021, 288 brands): TV advertising elasticities are substantially smaller than published estimates, with many insignificant or negative. Marginal ROI is negative for more than 80% of brands, implying over-investment, and the overall ROI of observed ad schedules is positive for only about a third of brands. Results are robust to model form and not driven by low power. Use to challenge TV budgets without lift evidence; US packaged goods context.
facts.source_title: TV Advertising Effectiveness and Profitability: Generalizable Results From 288 Brands (Econometrica)

facts.statement: Observational ad measurement vs experiments (Gordon, Zettelmeyer, Bhargava & Chapsky, Marketing Science 2019): across 15 US Facebook ad experiments (about 500 million user-experiment observations, 1.6 billion impressions), observational methods often failed to reproduce the randomized lift, even with rich demographic and behavioral controls and modern causal-inference methods. Use to require randomized lift tests before trusting attribution-based ROAS.
facts.source_title: A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook (Marketing Science)

facts.statement: Measuring ad returns is noisy (Lewis & Rao, QJE 2015): 25 large field experiments with US retailers and brokerages ($2.8M of digital ads, most reaching millions) had a median confidence interval on ROI over 100 percentage points wide; individual sales are so volatile (coefficient of variation around 10) that informative tests can need over 10 million person-weeks. Selection bias cripples observational methods. Use to set honest test sizes and to avoid over-reading small lift tests.
facts.source_title: The Unfavorable Economics of Measuring the Returns to Advertising (QJE)

facts.statement: Ghost ads (Johnson, Lewis & Nubbemeyer, JMR 2017): identifying the control-group users who would have seen an ad gives cleaner, cheaper lift tests than PSA or intent-to-treat designs and works with real-time optimizing ad platforms. In an online retailer's display retargeting campaign, ads lifted site visits by 17.2% and purchases by 10.5%, measured at least an order of magnitude more cheaply. Use when choosing lift-test designs; the lift figures are from one retailer.
facts.source_title: Ghost Ads: Improving the Economics of Measuring Online Ad Effectiveness (JMR)

facts.statement: Paid search incrementality at eBay (Blake, Nosko & Tadelis, Econometrica 2015): large field experiments showed returns from paid search are a fraction of non-experimental estimates. Brand-keyword ads had no measurable short-term benefit; non-brand ads positively influenced new and infrequent users, but frequent users, who would buy anyway, absorbed most spend, so average returns were negative. Use to test brand-term and loyal-user spend with holdouts; effects differ when competitors bid on your brand.
facts.source_title: Consumer Heterogeneity and Paid Search Effectiveness: A Large-Scale Field Experiment (Econometrica)

facts.statement: Brand keyword defense (Simonov, Nosko & Rao, Marketing Science 2018, Bing experiments, thousands of brands): with no competitors bidding, brand ads add only 1-4% clicks (less for big brands), so cost per incremental click is high. Competitors in paid positions 2-4 take 1-5% of clicks when the brand advertises, but 18-42% when the brand does not, making defensive brand bidding strongly ROI-positive when rivals bid. Use to decide brand-term bidding by checking competitor presence first.
facts.source_title: Competition and Crowd-Out for Brand Keywords in Sponsored Search (Marketing Science)

facts.statement: Dynamic retargeting (Lambrecht & Tucker, JMR 2013, online travel field experiment): ads showing the exact products a user viewed were on average less effective than generic brand ads. They stopped underperforming once browsing showed refined preferences (e.g., visiting review sites). Use to show generic or category creative to early-stage visitors and product-specific creative only to users deep in research. One travel firm, so test in your category.
facts.source_title: When Does Retargeting Work? Information Specificity in Online Advertising (JMR)

facts.statement: Targeting vs obtrusiveness (Goldfarb & Tucker, Marketing Science 2011, large field experiment): matching a display ad to page content and making an ad more obtrusive each raised purchase intent, but combining both performed worse than either alone. The penalty was strongest for privacy-sensitive people and categories. Use to avoid pairing tight contextual targeting with intrusive formats, especially in sensitive categories like health or finance.
facts.source_title: Online Display Advertising: Targeting and Obtrusiveness (Marketing Science)

facts.statement: Email personalization field experiments (Sahni, Wheeler & Chintagunta, Marketing Science 2018, millions of recipients, three companies): adding the recipient's name to the subject line raised open rate by 20% (9.05% to 10.80%), sales leads by 31% (0.39% to 0.51%) and cut unsubscribes by 17% (1.2% to 1.0%). Effects held for acquisition and retention emails. Use name personalization as a default test; it seems to work by raising attention to the rest of the message, not by adding information.
facts.source_title: Personalization in Email Marketing: The Role of Noninformative Advertising Content (Marketing Science)

facts.statement: Online reviews and sales (Chevalier & Mayzlin, JMR 2006, Amazon vs Barnes & Noble books): reviews are overwhelmingly positive; an improvement in a book's reviews raised its relative sales on that site; for most samples a one-star review hurt more than a five-star review helped; and review length data suggest buyers read text, not only averages. Use to prioritise responding to and fixing causes of negative reviews. Books, 2000s data.
facts.source_title: The Effect of Word of Mouth on Sales: Online Book Reviews (JMR)

facts.statement: eWOM elasticity meta-analysis (You, Vadakkepatt & Joshi, Journal of Marketing 2015; 51 studies, 339 volume and 271 valence elasticities): sales elasticity to review volume is 0.236 and to valence (rating) 0.417. Both are higher for privately consumed, low-trialability products in less competitive industries and for reviews on independent review sites. Use to estimate the payoff of review programmes; strongest for products buyers cannot try first.
facts.source_title: A Meta-Analysis of Electronic Word-of-Mouth Elasticity (Journal of Marketing)

facts.statement: eWOM and sales meta-analysis (Babic Rosario et al., JMR 2016; 1,532 effect sizes, 96 studies, 40 platforms, 26 categories): eWOM correlates positively with sales (average r = .091). Volume matters more than valence; negative eWOM does not always hurt sales, but high rating variability does. On social platforms, effects are stronger when receivers can judge similarity to senders. Use to aim review programmes at more reviews and consistent experience, not only a higher average.
facts.source_title: The Effect of Electronic Word of Mouth on Sales: A Meta-Analytic Review of Platform, Product, and Metric Factors (JMR)

facts.statement: Ad repetition meta-analysis (Schmidt & Eisend, Journal of Advertising 2015): in experimental settings, brand attitude peaks at about ten exposures, while recall rises linearly and does not level off before the eighth exposure. Spaced exposures and low involvement strengthen attitude effects; repetition effects decay over time. Use to set frequency caps and flighting (space exposures rather than bunching). Lab exposures are forced, so real-world in-feed needs may differ.
facts.source_title: Advertising Repetition: A Meta-Analysis on Effective Frequency in Advertising (Journal of Advertising)

facts.statement: Advertising response is usually convex (Taylor, Kennedy & Sharp, Journal of Advertising Research 2009): single-source data for brands in four consumer goods categories support the prior finding that convex (diminishing-returns) response functions are typical, though not universal. Implication: spreading budget for reach usually beats piling frequency on the same people. Use for media plans favouring reach and continuity; measurement issues and boundary conditions remain open.
facts.source_title: Is Once Really Enough? Making Generalizations about Advertising's Convex Sales Response Function (JAR)

facts.statement: TV split-cable tests (Lodish et al., JMR 1995, 389 BehaviorScan tests): many common beliefs did not separate effective from ineffective TV ads; increasing budgets relative to competitors did not increase sales in general, and standard recall and persuasion copy-test scores were weakly related to sales. Changing brand, copy or media strategy in categories with many purchase occasions and low in-store merchandising raised the odds of an effect. Use to demand in-market tests over copy-test scores.
facts.source_title: How T.V. Advertising Works: A Meta-Analysis of 389 Real World Split Cable T.V. Advertising Experiments (JMR)

facts.statement: Long-term TV effects (Lodish et al., Marketing Science 1995, 55 BehaviorScan weight tests for established packaged goods): when extra TV weight lifted sales significantly in year one, the first year's sales impact roughly doubled over the following two years on average, mainly through a higher buying rate in the test group. When year one showed no significant lift, there was none in the following two years either. Use to judge long-term effects only after a measurable short-term lift; CPG, pre-digital media.
facts.source_title: A Summary of Fifty-Five In-Market Experimental Estimates of the Long-Term Effect of TV Advertising (Marketing Science)

facts.statement: Update of real-world TV tests (Hu, Lodish & Krieger, JAR 2007; 241 IRI BehaviorScan and matched-market tests, 1989-2003): for established products, increasing TV weight improved sales effectiveness significantly above zero, unlike the 1995 study, driven mainly by more recent tests; average effectiveness rose for tests after 1995. The authors still advise identifying ad effectiveness before launching campaigns. Use to show weight increases can work when the ad itself is effective; US CPG data.
facts.source_title: An Analysis of Real World TV Advertising Tests: A 15-Year Update (JAR)

facts.statement: Long-term mix effects (Ataman, van Heerde & Mela, JMR 2010; 70 brands, 25 categories, 5 years, France): total (short plus long-term) sales elasticity was 1.37 for product and 0.74 for distribution, versus 0.13 for advertising and 0.04 for discounting. Discounting's long-term effect was one-third of its short-term effect, while other mix elements had long-term effects over four times their short-term ones. Use to push product and distribution before discounts for mature brands.
facts.source_title: The Long-Term Effect of Marketing Strategy on Brand Sales (JMR)

facts.statement: Price promotions have no permanent effect (Pauwels, Hanssens & Siddarth, JMR 2002, scanner panel, storable and perishable products): permanent promotion effects on category incidence, brand choice and purchase quantity were virtually absent. Over the adjustment period, the long-run decomposition was 66/11/23 (incidence/choice/quantity) for the storable product and 58/39/3 for the perishable one. Use to treat discounts as temporary volume, not lasting share growth.
facts.source_title: The Long-Term Effects of Price Promotions on Category Incidence, Brand Choice, and Purchase Quantity (JMR)

facts.statement: Promotions train price sensitivity (Mela, Gupta & Lehmann, JMR 1997, 8.25 years of panel data for a packaged good): consumers became more price- and promotion-sensitive over time, consistent with reduced advertising and increased promotions. Use to warn against habitual discounting: frequent deals can raise long-run price sensitivity and erode pricing power. Single-category evidence, so test before generalizing.
facts.source_title: The Long-Term Impact of Promotion and Advertising on Consumer Brand Choice (JMR)

facts.statement: Personal selling elasticity meta-analysis (Albers, Mantrala & Sridhar, JMR 2010; 506 estimates, 88 data sets, 75 articles): mean current-period sales elasticity to personal selling effort is 0.34 (about 0.31 after method-bias correction), higher for early life-cycle offerings and in Europe, and smaller in recent years. For rough comparison, Sethuraman et al. report a mean short-term ad elasticity of 0.12, but the two meta-analyses differ in construct and method. Use when weighing sales headcount vs media for B2B; estimates are sensitive to model choices.
facts.source_title: Personal Selling Elasticities: A Meta-Analysis (JMR)

facts.statement: Choice overload is not a general rule (Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd, JCR 2010): a meta-analysis of 63 conditions from 50 experiments (N=5,036) found a mean effect of virtually zero with large variance across studies, and no sufficient conditions for when more options hurt. Use to test assortment and plan-count changes rather than assuming fewer options always convert better.
facts.source_title: Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload (JCR)

facts.statement: When choice overload does occur (Chernev, Bockenholt & Goodman, JCP 2015; 99 observations, N=7,202): large assortments hurt choice when choice sets are complex, the decision task is difficult, preferences are uncertain, or buyers want to minimize effort; with these moderators accounted for, the assortment effect is significant. Use to simplify pricing pages and plan grids for novice or low-effort buyers, and to add recommendations or defaults when many options are needed.
facts.source_title: Choice overload: A conceptual review and meta-analysis (Journal of Consumer Psychology)

facts.statement: Zero price effect (Shampanier, Mazar & Ariely, Marketing Science 2007): when the price gap between two products is held constant, making the cheaper one free makes dramatically more people choose it and fewer choose the expensive option; people treat free as adding benefit, not just removing cost, with affect the likeliest explanation. Use to design free tiers, free trials and free-shipping offers; experiments with low-priced items, so test on your margins.
facts.source_title: Zero as a Special Price: The True Value of Free Products (Marketing Science)

facts.statement: Experimentation at scale (Kohavi et al., KDD 2013): Microsoft Bing ran over 200 concurrent controlled experiments a day; many ideas move key metrics by about 1% (worth over $10M a year in US revenue) yet are not well estimated in advance, and experiments caught many negative features stakeholders were excited about. Trustworthiness issues include frequent false positives and interactions between experiments. Use to justify testing over opinion and to guard against false positives.
facts.source_title: Online controlled experiments at large scale (KDD 2013)

facts.statement: Creative devices and sales (Hartnett et al., Journal of Advertising, 312 TV ads, several categories and countries): replicating Stewart and Furse's codebook of 150+ creative devices against in-market short-term sales, no single creative device did much alone to explain sales effectiveness, and the most and least effective devices differed from the original copy-test study. Use to avoid creative checklists as guarantees; test executions in market.
facts.source_title: Creative That Sells: How Advertising Execution Affects Sales (Journal of Advertising)

facts.statement: LinkedIn bans crawlers, bots, browser plug-ins and extensions that scrape LinkedIn, change how it looks, or automate activity. Its help page cites User Agreement section 8.2, which forbids bots or other unauthorized automated methods to access the Services or to add or download contacts. Members who use such tools risk restriction or closure of their account. Treat LinkedIn outreach as manual work by the founder: no automated connection requests, profile visits, messages or scraping tools.
facts.source_title: LinkedIn Help - Prohibited software and extensions

facts.statement: Gartner's press release of 9 Mar 2026 on a survey of 646 B2B buyers (fielded Aug-Sep 2025) reports that 67% prefer a rep-free buying experience and 45% used AI tools during a recent purchase. Gartner advises sellers to help buying groups reach value clarity. These are Gartner survey results about stated preference, not observed behaviour. Publish self-serve proof (pricing, ROI, comparisons, security docs) that buyers and their AI tools can find before any sales contact.
facts.source_title: Gartner Sales Survey Finds 67% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Experience

facts.statement: The FTC says CAN-SPAM makes no exception for business-to-business email. Every commercial email needs accurate header details, a subject line that doesn't mislead, a clear notice that it is an ad, a valid physical postal address and a clear opt-out covering all marketing mail. The opt-out must keep working for at least 30 days after sending, and requests must be honored within 10 business days. You stay liable for mail that third parties send for you. Each violating email can draw a penalty of up to $53,088.
facts.source_title: FTC - CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business

facts.statement: UK PECR B2B rule (ICO): you may email or text corporate subscribers (companies, LLPs, government bodies) without prior consent, but you should identify yourself and the ICO advises keeping a 'do not email or text' list of businesses that object. Sole traders and some partnerships are treated as individuals: email them only with specific consent or under the soft opt-in for past customers. The ICO says this guidance is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act and may change.
facts.source_title: ICO - Electronic mail marketing (Guide to PECR)

facts.statement: Germany has no B2B exemption for cold email. UWG section 7(2) no. 2 treats any email advertising sent without the recipient's prior express consent as an unreasonable nuisance, whether the recipient is a business or a consumer. The only exception, section 7(3), covers an existing customer whose address you got through a sale: you may then advertise your own similar goods or services until they object, and at collection and in every email you must tell them they can object at any time. Don't send cold sequences to German addresses without consent.
facts.source_title: Gesetz gegen den unlauteren Wettbewerb (UWG) section 7 - Unzumutbare Belaestigungen

facts.statement: France (CNIL): B2B email prospecting may rely on legitimate interest, without prior consent, if the message relates to the recipient's profession, and every message must identify the sender and offer a simple, free way to object. B2C email needs prior consent, apart from the existing-customer exception for similar products (an account alone, with no sale, doesn't qualify). Generic addresses like info@ or contact@ aren't covered by these rules. Pre-ticked consent boxes are banned.
facts.source_title: CNIL - La prospection commerciale par courrier electronique

facts.statement: LinkedIn Sponsored Messaging (Conversation and Message ads) has been able to target EU members since mid-October 2024, but only reaches EU members who opted in to ads in their inbox, and they can withdraw that consent. LinkedIn caps how often a member receives Sponsored Messaging but publishes no number. Ads are delivered only when members are active on LinkedIn, Conversation ads are archived 20-40 days after receipt, and each creative can link only one Lead Gen Form. Expect small EU reach and plan feed ads alongside.
facts.source_title: LinkedIn Marketing Solutions Help - Conversation ads

facts.statement: Australia's Spam Act (ACMA): every commercial email or SMS needs the recipient's express or inferred consent, and the sender must prove it. You can't send an email to ask for consent. Inferred consent needs an ongoing relationship the marketing directly relates to. A purchase alone doesn't count. Each message must identify the sender (legal name or ABN) with contact details valid for 30 days. The unsubscribe must be clear, free and need no login or extra data, work for 30 days, and be honored within 5 working days. Harvested lists are banned.
facts.source_title: ACMA - Avoid sending spam

facts.statement: GDPR recital 47 says direct marketing may be regarded as a legitimate interest, so B2B outreach to named people in the EU can rest on Art. 6(1)(f) where national e-privacy law allows it. Art. 21(2)-(3) gives an absolute right to object: once someone objects, stop all marketing processing of their data, profiling included. Art. 21(4) requires you to bring this right to their attention clearly and separately no later than the first communication, so put a plain opt-out line in the first cold email.
facts.source_title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) - Recital 47 and Article 21

facts.statement: LinkedIn Lead Gen Form leads: Campaign Manager now stores collected member profile data for one year (not 90 days, the old limit) under LinkedIn's member privacy policy. Metrics stay longer. Download per form (Content & Assets > Lead generation forms, choose dates) or per ad set (Export, report type Leads), or sync to a CRM. Downloading needs Viewer access or higher on the ad account plus Lead Gen Forms manager or higher on the Company Page. Send a test lead, and use hidden fields for campaign and source routing.
facts.source_title: LinkedIn Help - View and download leads, metrics, and analytics for Lead Gen Form campaigns

facts.statement: Sales Navigator InMail limits (LinkedIn Help): Core, Advanced and Advanced Plus users each get 50 InMail credits a month, renewed on the 1st (UTC). Unused credits roll over but expire after 90 days, the balance caps at 150, and you can't buy extra credits. A credit comes back when an InMail gets a reply within 90 days (auto-replies count). Unanswered InMails aren't refunded. Plan about 50 highly targeted InMails per seat per month and favor relevance over volume.
facts.source_title: LinkedIn Sales Navigator Help - InMail crediting and renewal process

facts.statement: RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe, technical details: the List-Unsubscribe header must contain one HTTPS URI (mailto may be added), and List-Unsubscribe-Post must carry exactly 'List-Unsubscribe=One-Click'. The message needs a valid DKIM signature that covers both headers. The endpoint must accept a POST that has no cookies, HTTP auth or other context, and must not answer with a redirect, because browsers often turn redirected POSTs into GETs. Test the endpoint with a bare POST before every new sending domain goes live.
facts.source_title: RFC 8058 - Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers

facts.statement: Gmail BIMI (Google Workspace Admin Help): to show a brand logo, the domain's DMARC policy must be p=quarantine or p=reject with pct=100 (p=none isn't supported), and you need a Verified Mark Certificate (VMC, needs a trademarked logo, can take 6-12 months) or a Common Mark Certificate (CMC). The logo must be SVG Tiny PS (baseProfile tiny-ps, version 1.2), at least 96x96 px with absolute size, delivered in a PEM file. Only VMC senders get Gmail's checkmark.
facts.source_title: Google Workspace Admin Help - Set up BIMI

facts.statement: Apple Mail Privacy Protection ('Protect Mail Activity' in Mail settings) hides the recipient's IP address and downloads remote content privately in the background when a message arrives, not when it is opened. Senders therefore can't learn whether or when a message was opened. Treat open rates from Apple Mail users as inflated and unreliable: don't use opens for A/B winners, engagement-based sunsetting or send-time optimisation. Use clicks, replies and conversions instead.
facts.source_title: Apple Mail User Guide - Protect email privacy

facts.statement: Google's recommended DMARC rollout: set up SPF and DKIM at least 48 hours before DMARC. Start with p=none for one week and review the reports daily. If outgoing mail shows no problems, quarantine a small share of messages (large organizations can start at 1%) and raise the percentage gradually to 100%. Use p=reject only if needed, because failing mail is then never delivered. Move to enforcement this way before applying for BIMI, which needs quarantine or reject at 100%.
facts.source_title: Google Workspace Admin Help - Recommended DMARC rollout

facts.statement: DMARCbis was published in May 2026 as RFC 9989 (Standards Track), obsoleting RFC 7489 and RFC 9091, with RFC 9990 (aggregate reports) and RFC 9991 (failure reports). Organizational domains are now found with a 'DNS Tree Walk' of up to eight queries instead of the Public Suffix List. The pct, rf and ri tags are removed, and t=y (testing) replaces pct=0. A new np tag sets policy for non-existent subdomains, and psd flags public suffix domains. v=DMARC1 records still work, but drop pct and set np=reject on brand domains.
facts.source_title: RFC 9989 - Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)

facts.statement: Gmail Postmaster Tools v2 has a Compliance status dashboard. For all senders it checks SPF, DKIM, DNS records, formatting, encryption and the user-reported spam rate. For bulk senders (about 5,000+ messages to Gmail in 24 hours) it also checks DMARC, one-click unsubscribe and whether unsubscribes are honored within 48 hours. Status reads Compliant, Needs work or No data found, for primary domains and personal Gmail traffic only. Data usually updates within 24 hours, but fixes can take up to 7 days to show.
facts.source_title: Gmail Help - Postmaster Tools dashboards

facts.statement: Gmail Postmaster Tools lets verified domain owners report a delivery issue (Report delivery issue, bottom left). The domain must meet Google's sender guidelines, and the message you report must pass both DKIM and SPF with a From: header domain matching the domain you send from. Fix authentication and compliance before using this route.
facts.source_title: Gmail Help - Report delivery issues in Postmaster Tools

facts.statement: Gmail's sender guidelines say: use a consistent From: address for each message category (for example sales receipts, promotions, account alerts). Ideally send from one IP; if you use several, assign a different IP to each message type. Don't mix content types, such as promotions inside receipts. New senders should start with low volume to engaged users and increase slowly, avoiding sudden spikes. Don't impersonate Gmail From: headers: Gmail is moving toward DMARC quarantine enforcement for them.
facts.source_title: Gmail Help - Email sender guidelines

facts.statement: Microsoft 365 business mailboxes give every inbound message a bulk complaint level (BCL) from 0 to 9. At or above the tenant's threshold, newsletters and promotions are treated as Bulk and by default go to Junk, even when recipients opted in. Some tenants can send bulk mail below the threshold to a Promotions folder (preview). B2B senders can't change a recipient's threshold: keep complaints low, send only to engaged contacts, and ask key accounts to add you to Safe Senders.
facts.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Anti-spam protection FAQ (Defender for Office 365)

facts.statement: Microsoft's outbound best practices for mail to Microsoft 365: the sending domain must resolve in DNS, or mail goes via the high-risk delivery pool. The IP needs a reverse DNS (PTR) record. HELO/EHLO and MAIL FROM should use a consistent domain name matching rDNS, not an IP. Publish SPF, sign DKIM with relaxed header canonicalization, keep WHOIS accurate, format bounces per RFC 3464, remove addresses that hard-bounce, and monitor IPs in Outlook.com SNDS.
facts.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Anti-spam protection FAQ: best practices for outbound mail

facts.statement: UK Data (Use and Access) Act 2025: the ICO says that as of 19 Jun 2026 all of the Act's data protection provisions are in force. Some cookies, such as those used for statistics or basic website functionality, can be set without consent. Charities get an email soft opt-in for people who engaged with their work. The Act's clearer drafting also confirms that direct marketing can be a legitimate interest. The ICO's PECR guidance is flagged as under review, so check before dropping UK cookie consent for analytics tags.
facts.source_title: ICO - The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025: what does it mean for organisations?

facts.statement: The EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854) has applied since 12 Sep 2025, says the European Commission. Users of connected products can access the data they generate and share it with third parties such as repair providers. The Act prohibits unfair contract terms that could prevent data-sharing, and customers can move data and switch between cloud providers. Products, apps or SaaS tied to devices need data-access flows and contract terms that comply.
facts.source_title: European Commission - Data Act

facts.statement: Global Privacy Control (GPC) is a proposed specification, delivered by a browser setting or extension, that lets users signal their privacy preferences to sites. Its site frames it as a Do Not Sell or Share request under the CCPA and as a general request under GDPR Articles 7 and 21. GPC became an official work item of the W3C Privacy Working Group in Nov 2024 and is still being standardised. Treat a detected GPC signal as an opt-out of sale/sharing and switch off those tags for that visitor.
facts.source_title: Global Privacy Control

facts.statement: Maryland Online Data Privacy Act (Ch. 455, 2024) took effect 1 Oct 2025 (one section applies only to processing from 1 Apr 2026). It covers firms handling data of 35,000+ Maryland consumers, or 10,000+ with over 20% of revenue from selling data. Sensitive data may be collected or processed only when strictly necessary for a product the consumer requested, and its sale is banned. Targeted ads to, and data sales about, consumers the controller knows or should know are under 18 are banned. A 60-day cure period runs to 1 Apr 2027.
facts.source_title: Maryland 2024 Laws Ch. 455 (SB 541) - Maryland Online Data Privacy Act of 2024

facts.statement: Indiana's Consumer Data Protection Act has applied since 1 Jan 2026, enforced by the Attorney General. It covers businesses that operate in Indiana or target its residents and that process data of 100,000+ Indiana residents, or of 25,000+ residents with more than 50% of gross revenue from selling personal data. Consumers can access, correct, delete and port their data and opt out of targeted advertising, sale and profiling. Controllers must answer requests within 45 days, with extensions allowed.
facts.source_title: Indiana Attorney General - Consumer Data Protection Consumer Bill of Rights

facts.statement: The Tennessee Information Protection Act took effect 1 Jul 2025. It applies to businesses with over $25M annual revenue that also process data of 175,000+ Tennessee consumers a year, or of 25,000+ with 50% of revenue from selling data. Consumers can opt out of sale, targeted advertising and profiling, and requests get an answer within 45 days. Before acting, the AG must give 60 days to cure. A written privacy program that reasonably conforms to the NIST Privacy Framework is an affirmative defense.
facts.source_title: Tennessee Attorney General - Guidance on the Tennessee Information Protection Act

facts.statement: Connecticut Data Privacy Act (AG guidance): it applies to controllers processing data of 35,000+ consumers, to anyone processing sensitive data or selling personal data, and to all consumer health data controllers. Since 1 Jan 2025, every covered controller must honor opt-out preference signals such as Global Privacy Control for targeted ads and sales. Sensitive data needs consent. Selling data of, or targeting ads to, consumers under 16 needs opt-in consent, and online services may not target ads to known minors under 18. Profiling needs an impact assessment.
facts.source_title: Connecticut Attorney General - The Connecticut Data Privacy Act

facts.statement: India notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules on 14 Nov 2025 with an 18-month phased compliance period, so most obligations bind from about May 2027. The rules cover consent notices, verifiable parental consent for children's data, breach reporting and registered Consent Managers. Maximum penalties under the Act reach Rs 250 crore for failing reasonable security safeguards and Rs 200 crore for breach-notice or child-data failures, with lower tiers for other violations (Rs 50 crore for general non-compliance).
facts.source_title: PIB backgrounder - DPDP Rules, 2025 Notified

facts.statement: Brazil LGPD transfers: ANPD Resolution CD/ANPD 19/2024 (published 23 Aug 2024) regulates international data transfers. Exporters relying on contracts had up to 12 months, to about 23 Aug 2025, to add ANPD's standard contractual clauses to their contracts. The resolution also sets procedures for specific clauses, global corporate rules and adequacy decisions. Any marketing tool or processor that sends Brazilian personal data abroad, such as US-hosted CRM, email or ads platforms, now needs ANPD's clauses in its DPA.
facts.source_title: ANPD - ANPD aprova regulamento sobre transferencias internacionais de dados

facts.statement: Under TikTok's Community Guidelines (released 25 Aug 2026, effective 24 Sep 2026), content is ineligible for the For You feed if it includes unoriginal or reused material without anything new. Content that tries to manipulate people into giving gifts or inflating likes or follows is also ineligible. Add something new when you repurpose clips.
facts.source_title: TikTok Community Guidelines: Integrity and Authenticity
