facts.statement: On 15 Jul 2025 YouTube renamed its 'repetitious content' monetization policy to 'inauthentic content' and clarified that it covers mass-produced or repetitive videos, such as content made from templates with minimal variation between videos. Such channels can't monetize. The separate 'reused content' policy, which covers clips, compilations and reaction videos without meaningful commentary or added value, was not changed.
facts.source_title: YouTube channel monetization policies (YouTube Help)

facts.statement: LinkedIn Help (page current as of Nov 2026) says LinkedIn may cap how many comments a member or Page can post in a given time period. If it detects excessive comment creation or use of an automation tool, it may limit the visibility of those comments. Members can also restrict comments on their posts to connections only. Plan comment-first engagement manually and at a human pace, with no auto-commenting tools.
facts.source_title: LinkedIn Help: commenting on posts

facts.statement: X's open-sourced For You algorithm (xai-org/x-algorithm, README last updated 26 Oct 2026) ranks posts with a transformer model, Phoenix. The score is a weighted sum of predicted action probabilities, with negative actions such as mute, block and report carrying negative weights. After scoring, repeat posts from the same author are decayed, posts from accounts the viewer doesn't follow are discounted, and a New-Author Boost lifts authors whose impressions are below a threshold. An age filter removes posts older than 48 hours.
facts.source_title: xai-org/x-algorithm (GitHub README)

facts.statement: Meta's Threads Feed system card (updated 7 Mar 2025) says the feed blends content from accounts you follow with recommended content. Ranking models use signals such as your engagement with similar accounts and topics, recent likes, follows and time spent viewing posts, and one predictor uses a post's ratio of likes to impressions. Choosing Hide reduces similar content, and reporting a post shows you less like it. The Following tab shows only accounts you follow, in reverse chronological order.
facts.source_title: Meta Transparency Center: Threads Feed AI system

facts.statement: Since 16 Oct 2025, Pinterest users can choose to see less GenAI content on eligible image Pins in categories prone to AI generation: beauty, art, fashion and home decor (initial controls also covered architecture, entertainment, health and sport). Food and drink was added 12 Dec 2025. The setting is under 'refine your recommendations' or the Pin's three-dot menu. GenAI labels on image Pins that Pinterest flags as AI-made or AI-edited become more visible as detection improves. AI-heavy Pins in these categories may reach fewer people.
facts.source_title: Pinterest rolls out new tools to give users more control over GenAI content

facts.statement: On 31 Oct 2025 Bluesky said a newer model flags toxic, spammy, off-topic or bad-faith replies and down-ranks them in reply threads, search results and notifications. It is building 'social neighborhood' ranking that gives priority to replies from people closer to the viewer. It also plans to test a private 'dislike' signal to personalize Discover and other feeds. Brand replies should be on-topic and come from accounts with real ties to the community.
facts.source_title: Progress Update: Building Healthier Social Media (Bluesky blog)

facts.statement: Meta's Instagram Explore system card (updated 22 Jun 2026) describes staged ranking. Retrieval gathers up to 1,500 candidates from accounts you engage with and posts similar to what you engaged with. A two-tower neural network narrows these to 100. A multi-task model then ranks them on predicted engagement, including the chance you spend more than five seconds viewing a post or watch more than 95% of a video. Users can tune Explore with 'Tune Your Algorithm'.
facts.source_title: Meta Transparency Center: Instagram Explore AI system

facts.statement: Google's Ads developer blog (21 Oct 2026) announces that from 4 Dec 2026 image extraction is on by default for newly created Performance Max campaigns, even where dynamic images were turned off at account level. Existing campaigns keep their settings, per press coverage of the post. To keep brand control, opt out of GENERATE_IMAGE_EXTRACTION in asset_automation_settings when creating new PMax campaigns, and confirm the exact enum value in Google's docs.
facts.source_title: Upcoming changes to image extraction in Performance Max campaigns starting December 4, 2026 (Google Ads Developer Blog)

facts.statement: Google Ads API v26 was released on 14 Oct 2026, with v26.1 on 28 Oct 2026. Google's schedule lists these sunsets: v23.x in Feb 2027, v24.x in May 2027 (v24.2 in Jun 2027), v25.x in Aug 2027 and v26.x in Nov 2027. Keep integrations on a supported version and schedule migrations well before each sunset.
facts.source_title: Google Ads API release and sunset dates; Google Ads API Release and Sunset Schedules for 2026-2027

facts.statement: Google Ads API v26 (14 Oct 2026) adds a require_eu_political_advertising_declaration field on geo target constants and criteria, so you can tell when the EU political advertising declaration is needed. Clearly non-EU campaigns no longer need it, but only for code running on v26. v26 also adds 15 Search Lift metrics. Check the v26 release notes before changing declaration logic.
facts.source_title: Announcing v26 of the Google Ads API

facts.statement: Google widened its Limited Ad Serving policy to all Google Ads from August 2026 (posted 5 Aug 2026; gradual rollout through 2028). Google may cap impressions for advertisers it sees as not yet qualified, judged on account maturity, verification, policy history, user reports and industry. Ads aren't disapproved and only accounts with a meaningful share of affected impressions are notified. On Search, make the brand clear in ads and landing pages, avoid generic copy, and complete advertiser verification.
facts.source_title: Update to Limited Ad Serving Policy (August 2026)

facts.statement: From 21 Jul 2026, Google Ads no longer lets you appeal a policy decision from your account if the decision is more than 6 months old. Log every disapproval or suspension with its date and file appeals well within 6 months.
facts.source_title: Update to Appeals Limits (July 2026)

facts.statement: From July 2026 (posted 9 Jul 2026), Google lets advertisers label image and video creatives made or edited with AI, either directly or via the AI label setting in Google Ads, DV360, CM360, Merchant Center and Ads Editor. Labels that follow the update don't break text-overlay or watermark rules. Google may auto-label assets from its own AI tools. The setting doesn't guarantee legal compliance; Google cites EU, India and New York disclosure rules. Election ads still need the 'Altered or synthetic content' checkbox.
facts.source_title: Updates to AI labeling requirements (July 2026)

facts.statement: Microsoft Advertising (28 Oct 2026): messaging guidelines are in open pilot for Performance Max and for Search campaigns with AI Max. You can give AI-generated ad copy up to 40 guidelines on claims, themes, tone and words to avoid. Load claims.md rules and banned phrases there before turning on AI copy. The same update lets new advertisers build a first Performance Max campaign from sign-up using AI, with budget, bids, copy and assets editable before launch.
facts.source_title: Build, steer, and measure your campaigns with AI: What's new in Microsoft Advertising this October

facts.statement: Microsoft Advertising's September 2026 update post (dated 30 Sep 2026) says optimization experiments are generally available for Search, Shopping, Audience and Performance Max campaigns. A unified results page compares the experiment with the original setup side by side, and a winning change can be applied to the original campaign or used to start a new one. Microsoft advises testing now so campaigns have a stable baseline before holiday demand peaks.
facts.source_title: Microsoft Advertising blog - Less busywork, more growth: what's new this September

facts.statement: Meta Marketing API v26.0 (29 Jul 2026) breaking changes, applied to all versions on 27 Oct 2026: poll ads (poll_spec) are no longer accepted. Web and App campaigns can't use applink_treatment=web_only (use automatic or deeplink_with_web_fallback). Delivery Estimate fields daily_outcomes_curve, budget_guardrail and estimate_dau are removed. Housing, employment and financial (HEF) ad sets with custom audience or detailed targeting must set advantage_audience explicitly or the API errors.
facts.source_title: Marketing API changelog: Version 26.0

facts.statement: Meta Marketing API v26.0 targeting and placement changes: since 1 Sep 2026 (all versions) Lookalike country and location_spec are ignored, so lookalikes are countryless and delivery follows the ad set's locations. Messenger Stories was removed from all versions in late August 2026 and stripped from campaigns automatically. Instagram Explore Feed is no longer available from v26.0. Set geography on the ad set, not on the lookalike, and remove old placement values from manual placement specs.
facts.source_title: Marketing API changelog: Version 26.0

facts.statement: Meta ads in WhatsApp Status: the placement runs only with Instagram Stories also selected (standalone Status campaigns are not supported). Formats are single image, single video or carousel (up to 10 cards); collection and flexible formats are unavailable. A/B tests, Dynamic Creative, Reach and Frequency buying and Advantage+ Creative don't work there. user_age_unknown defaults to true, so creative must suit all ages. A WhatsApp identity can be set via wamo_whatsapp_identity_spec (new in v26.0).
facts.source_title: Ads in WhatsApp Status (Meta Marketing API documentation)

facts.statement: Threads ads via Meta's Marketing API need a Threads account that is Instagram-associated, Instagram-backed or Page-backed, and at least an Advertiser role on the Page linked to your Instagram account. Instagram-associated Threads accounts created before 29 Jan 2026 were added to the Business Portfolio automatically; newer ones must be added by hand. Only image, video and carousel formats work, ads can't be created from existing Threads posts, and Meta keeps Threads ad volume intentionally low during testing, so expect limited delivery.
facts.source_title: Threads Ads (Meta Marketing API documentation)

facts.statement: Meta Marketing API access changes (changelog entry dated 05/04/2026): 'Ads Management Standard Access' is now 'Marketing API Access Tier', with tiers renamed Limited access and Full access. Auto-approval for Full access drops from 1,500 to 500 Marketing API calls in 15 days, with error rate measured over a rolling 500-request window (must stay under 15%). Screen recordings are no longer needed for tier upgrades.
facts.source_title: Marketing API changelog (Meta for Developers)

facts.statement: TikTok is removing Custom Identity (ads with a custom display name and image and no linked account) from Ads Manager in early 2026, per its 22 Jan 2026 post. After that, all new campaigns must launch from a verified TikTok profile. Set up a Business or Organization Account, link it in Business Center, assign roles and run Spark Ads. Restricted verticals (alcohol, gambling, healthcare) follow a separate guide. TikTok gave no exact cutoff or rule for in-flight campaigns.
facts.source_title: Still using Custom Identity? Transition to a TikTok F.I.R.S.T. presence

facts.statement: Pinterest (19 Mar 2026) recommends Performance+ as the default campaign setup. It says its internal tests showed 10%+ better CPC and CPA than traditional setups, and that Performance+ beat traditional setups in 78% of A/B comparisons (no sample size given, so treat these as vendor figures). Advice: launch with the defaults, A/B test one lower-funnel or catalogue-sales campaign against your current setup, then scale the winner. New breakdowns by age, gender, geography, placement and device are available.
facts.source_title: Make Pinterest Performance+ campaigns your new default

facts.statement: Googlebot fetches only the first 2MB of an HTML page or other URL (PDFs: 64MB; crawlers with no stated limit: 15MB). The 2MB includes HTTP response headers (corrected 29 Oct 2026). Bytes past the cutoff are not fetched, rendered or indexed, and the truncated file is processed as if complete. Each script, stylesheet or XHR has its own 2MB counter. Keep HTML lean, move heavy inline CSS/JS to external files, and put title, meta robots, canonical and key structured data near the top. Published 31 Mar 2026.
facts.source_title: Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process

facts.statement: On 31 Mar 2026 Google moved its crawler IP range files from developers.google.com/search/apis/ipranges/ to developers.google.com/crawling/ipranges/, because the ranges cover more than Search crawlers. The old path still works for now but Google said it will redirect old locations to the new ones within 6 months. Update firewall rules, WAF allowlists, bot-verification scripts and log monitoring to read the new /crawling/ipranges/ path.
facts.source_title: New Location for the Google Crawlers' IP Range Files

facts.statement: Since 17 Nov 2025 Search Console lets you add custom annotations to Performance report charts: right-click the chart, choose 'Add annotation', give a date and a note of up to 120 characters. Every user with access to the property can see them, so keep personal data out. Log migrations, template changes, content refreshes, new agencies or plugins, and outside events (holidays, core updates) so traffic changes can be tied to causes.
facts.source_title: Adding context to your Search Console data with custom annotations

facts.statement: Search Console Insights has a 'Queries leading to your site' card with Query groups (announced 27 Oct 2025, gradual rollout). AI clusters phrasings, misspellings and languages with the same intent into groups showing total clicks, sorted into Top, Trending up and Trending down; clicking a group opens the Performance report with its queries. Only properties with a large query volume get it, groups can change over time, and they don't affect ranking. Use groups to plan topics, not exact keywords.
facts.source_title: Introducing Query groups in Search Console Insights

facts.statement: From 4 Dec 2025 Google began a limited, experimental rollout of AI-powered configuration in the Search Console Performance report: you type the analysis you want in plain language and it sets filters (query, page, country, device, search appearance, date), comparisons and which of the four metrics show. It works only in the Search results report, not Discover or News, can't sort or export, and can misread requests, so always check the filters it applied before trusting the numbers.
facts.source_title: Streamline your Search Console analysis with the new AI-powered configuration

facts.statement: Since 10 Dec 2025 the Search Console Performance report (Search results, Google News and Discover) has a granularity drop-down: Daily (default), weekly or monthly. Weekly or monthly views smooth daily swings and make date-range comparisons fairer, because day-of-week mismatches stop distorting the chart. Exports may change file and tab names, some column headers and sort order to match the chosen granularity. Available globally to all properties.
facts.source_title: Introducing weekly and monthly views in Search Console

facts.statement: On 24 Sep 2026 Google began rolling out multimodal search reporting globally in Search Console. A new multimodal search type filter appears in the Performance report for Search results and in the Generative AI features report. It covers image-based searches: Google Lens, Circle to Search on Android, image uploads to Google Search and Chrome's 'Search this image'. Data appears only if the site gets this traffic. Use it to judge how product and visual pages perform in image-led search.
facts.source_title: Announcing web multimodal Search performance reporting in Search Console

facts.statement: Anthropic runs three bots, and each can be blocked separately in robots.txt. ClaudeBot collects content that may be used for model training, so blocking it excludes your future content from training. Claude-SearchBot indexes content to improve Claude's search results, so blocking it can reduce your visibility there. Claude-User fetches pages when a Claude user asks a question, so blocking it stops those user-requested retrievals. Anthropic says its bots honor robots.txt and the non-standard Crawl-delay directive. Page dated 7 Apr 2026.
facts.source_title: Does Anthropic crawl data from the web, and how can site owners block the crawler?

facts.statement: Applebot crawls for Spotlight, Siri and Safari search features, and its data may also help train Apple's generative AI models. Applebot-Extended doesn't crawl: it only controls how Apple uses data Applebot has already crawled, so disallow Applebot-Extended in robots.txt to opt out of training. Applebot-Extended rules don't affect search ranking. The nosnippet directive keeps content out of AI-generated answers.
facts.source_title: About Applebot

facts.statement: Bing Webmaster Tools added an AI Performance report (public preview, 10 Feb 2026). It shows citations across Microsoft Copilot, AI-generated summaries in Bing and some partner integrations: total citations, average cited pages per day, grounding queries (the phrases the AI used to retrieve your content, sampled), page-level citation counts and trends. Citation counts aren't importance, ranking, placement, clicks or traffic. Use it to find indexed pages that are rarely cited and improve them, and use IndexNow so updates are picked up quickly.
facts.source_title: Introducing AI Performance in Bing Webmaster Tools Public Preview

facts.statement: On 16 Jun 2026 Bing added four preview features to AI Performance in Webmaster Tools. Intents sorts grounding queries into types such as Informational, Commercial, Navigational, Research and Local. Topics groups related queries into clusters. Citation Share is your site's citations as a percentage of all citations shown for the same grounding query. Compare overlays an earlier period on the current one. Bing says Citation Share is not a ranking or competitive scoreboard, shows no competitor domains, and can shift with model or freshness changes.
facts.source_title: New AI Visibility Insights in Bing Webmaster Tools: Intents, Topics, Citation Share, Compare

facts.statement: On 13 Oct 2026 Bing added Topics Portfolio (beta) to AI Performance in Webmaster Tools, for sites with enough data. It groups the grounding queries you're cited for into topics and shows each topic's size (total citations across all sites), the number of sites cited and the query count. Detail pages list opportunity queries, where other sites are cited and yours isn't, with volumes given as ranges. Classification is AI-generated and the numbers are directional. Start with topics where you're already cited, then target the opportunity queries.
facts.source_title: Introducing Topics Portfolio (Beta) in AI Performance

facts.statement: On 11 Jan 2026 Google launched the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), an open standard for agentic commerce co-developed with Shopify, Etsy, Wayfair, Target and Walmart. It works with A2A, AP2 and MCP. Its first use is native checkout on eligible Google listings in AI Mode and Gemini, paid with Google Pay (PayPal planned), starting with eligible US retailers. Retailers stay the seller of record and use their existing Merchant Center feeds. Google also announced dozens of new Merchant Center attributes for conversational shopping (product Q&A, accessories, substitutes).
facts.source_title: New tech and tools for retailers to succeed in an agentic shopping era

facts.statement: OpenAI's product feed spec for ChatGPT accepts JSONL, CSV or TSV. Discovery requires item_id, title, description, url, brand, seller_name, image_url, availability and price. is_eligible_search defaults to true, and setting it false also blocks checkout. Checkout needs a separately onboarded integration plus seller_privacy_policy and seller_tos. Ads stay off unless a feed-level default enables them. Update prices and availability when they change; sale or availability dates in the feed don't schedule anything. Spec read 3 Nov 2026.
facts.source_title: OpenAI Commerce: Product feed spec

facts.statement: Experience curve (Bruce Henderson, BCG, 1968): unit costs tend to fall by a steady 20-30% each time accumulated volume doubles, in constant dollars, but only when management actively drives costs down. Implication Henderson drew: share leaders gain a structural cost edge, so pricing a new product low enough to win its segment can pay off. Use it in growth work to test whether volume-led share plays and penetration pricing are justified by real scale economies, not as a law that holds automatically.
facts.source_title: The Experience Curve (BCG Classics, Bruce Henderson)

facts.statement: Adaptive advantage (Martin Reeves and Mike Deimler, BCG, HBR July-August 2011): classic strategy assumes a stable, predictable world, but the volatility of operating margins has more than doubled since 1980 and the gap between winners and losers has widened, so the ability to adapt (learn fast through experimentation and organizational learning) becomes a source of advantage in its own right. Use it to justify test-and-learn budgets and short planning cycles in volatile categories rather than fixed annual plans.
facts.source_title: Adaptability: The New Competitive Advantage (HBR)

facts.statement: BCG personalization framework (Mark Abraham and David Edelman, book 'Personalized: Customer Strategy in the Age of AI', HBR Press): personalization is framed as five promises a company makes to customers, Empower Me, Know Me, Reach Me, Show Me and Delight Me, each combining a human touch with technology, and BCG calls it a $2 trillion opportunity. Use the five promises as an audit checklist for a personalization roadmap: data and consent, targeting, channel reach, relevant content, and moments that surprise.
facts.source_title: Personalized: Customer Strategy in the Age of AI (BCG)

facts.statement: BCG Personalization Index (June 11, 2025; covers 200 brands across seven sectors): only about 10% of companies qualify as personalization leaders, and leaders achieve compound annual growth rates about 10% higher than laggards. This is cross-sectional, so it shows association rather than proof that personalization caused the growth. Use it to frame the upside of a personalization program, not to forecast a specific lift.
facts.source_title: The BCG Personalization Index: How Customer Experience Is Changing Across Industries in the Age of AI

facts.statement: BCG retail personalization (November 18, 2024): retail personalization leaders show revenue growth about 10 percentage points above laggards; returns on personalized offers run as much as three times those of mass promotions, yet retailers on average put under 5% of promotional spend into personalized offers. One large convenience chain raised personalized offers from 1% to 10% of investment, generating about $250 million in incremental sales. Use it to argue for shifting promo budget from blanket discounts to targeted offers, tested with holdouts.
facts.source_title: Retail Spotlight: Personalization in Action (BCG)

facts.statement: BCG 'Where's the Value in AI?' (press release October 24, 2024; survey of 1,000 CxOs and senior executives in 59 countries across ten major industries; executive opinion data): 74% of companies had not yet shown tangible value from AI, 26% had capabilities to move past proofs of concept, and 4% were at the cutting edge. About 62% of AI value came from core functions, with sales and marketing at 20%. Roughly 70% of AI challenges were people and process issues, 20% technology, 10% algorithms.
facts.source_title: AI Adoption in 2024: 74% of Companies Struggle to Achieve and Scale Value (BCG press release)

facts.statement: BCG 'The Widening AI Value Gap' (September 30, 2025; global executive research, sample size not stated on the article page): about 5% of firms are 'future-built' and capture AI value at scale, 35% are scaling and starting to see value, and 60% report hardly any material value despite real investment. Future-built firms report about five times the AI-driven revenue gains and three times the cost reductions of others. Use it as a reality check before promising AI marketing ROI: most companies are still in the no-value group.
facts.source_title: Are You Generating Value from AI? The Widening Gap (BCG)

facts.statement: BCG AI at Work 2025 (June 2025; survey of more than 10,600 leaders, managers and frontline white-collar staff in 11 countries and regions): over three quarters of leaders and managers use gen AI several times a week, but frontline regular use stalls at about 51%. Regular use is much higher where employees get at least five hours of training plus in-person coaching, yet only about a third say they were properly trained. Only 13% see agents deeply built into daily work. Budget training hours, not just licenses, for marketing and sales AI rollouts.
facts.source_title: AI at Work 2025: Momentum Builds, but Gaps Remain (BCG)

facts.statement: BCG annual CMO survey on gen AI (press release June 2, 2025; about 200 CMOs in Asia, Europe and North America, fielded April-May 2025; opinion data): 83% are optimistic about gen AI, up from 74% in 2023; 71% plan to spend over $10 million a year on it over the next three years, up from 57%; 60% expect revenue gains of 5% or more in focus areas; 30% name video generation as the next content focus; about a third of B2B and nearly a quarter of B2C CMOs rank AI agents as a high investment priority. Using gen AI to measure marketing ROI ranked last.
facts.source_title: CMO Confidence in GenAI Is Higher Than Ever, with Over 80% Expressing Optimism (BCG press release)

facts.statement: BCG with Yale, 'Agentic AI Will Make the CMO's Role More Consequential' (July 2026): AI agents judge brands on observable performance more than on marketing claims, so the brand promise must match the delivered experience. In BCG's annual survey of nearly 300 CMOs (opinion data), 96% say AI is driving end-to-end marketing transformation but only about a third have moved beyond basics, and 31% report agentic execution as a reality. BCG also reports 43% of consumer journeys are research-led and AI users rank AI tools among their top five influential touchpoints (85%).
facts.source_title: Agentic AI Will Make the CMO's Role More Consequential (BCG)

facts.statement: BCG '2027 Revenue Agenda' (October 19, 2026; survey of 398 CROs, sales, commercial and RevOps leaders at large companies in 23 countries; opinion data): 90% report meaningful AI use in sales workflows but only 6% run autonomous end-to-end deployments. Reported gains are mostly operational (33% less admin, 18% better forecasts) while only 13% cite win rates, 14% conversion and 8% quota attainment as top measured impacts. 81% set AI adoption goals but only 36% have formal targets and tracking. Point sales AI at buyer-facing proof of value and track revenue metrics, not just usage.
facts.source_title: The 2027 Revenue Agenda: Moving the AI Focus from Productivity to Proof of Value (BCG)

facts.statement: BCG 'How AI Agents Will Transform B2B Sales' (October 2025; BCG Center for Customer Insight survey of 400 US sales reps and managers): about seven in ten sellers already use general-purpose AI tools for emails, call summaries and follow-ups, but more than four in five cite inaccuracy and poor data integration, forcing manual double-checks, and about three in four feel under-supported by infrequent training. Fix CRM data quality and coaching before layering agents onto a sales team.
facts.source_title: How AI Agents Will Transform B2B Sales (BCG)

facts.statement: Net Promoter Score (Fred Reichheld with a Bain team; introduced in HBR, December 2003, 'The One Number You Need to Grow'): ask how likely a customer is to recommend you to a friend or colleague on a 0-10 scale; 9-10 are promoters, 7-8 passives, 0-6 detractors; NPS = % promoters minus % detractors. The team found this question predicted repurchase and referral best in most mature, competitive industries, then added a follow-up 'why?' that grew into the Net Promoter System. Use it as a relationship metric paired with the open-text reason, not as a standalone growth predictor.
facts.source_title: The History of Net Promoter (Bain & Company, netpromotersystem.com)

facts.statement: Net Promoter System inner loop, the 'closed loop' (Rob Markey, Bain, April 2015): route each piece of customer feedback quickly to every employee who shaped that experience, at the smallest practical team level and while it is fresh; call back customers when issues are unresolved or they are angry; and use supervisors or peers to coach on what to try next. The purpose is learning, not ranking, and Bain argues against tying this feedback to pay. Use it to design survey follow-up workflows so NPS turns into fixes rather than a dashboard number.
facts.source_title: The Net Promoter System's Inner Loop (Bain)

facts.statement: Net Promoter 3.0 and Earned Growth (Fred Reichheld, Darci Darnell and Maureen Burns, HBR, October 2021; book 'Winning on Purpose'): because NPS gets gamed when frontline bonuses are tied to scores, Bain added Earned Growth, an accounting-based counterpart to NPS built on audited revenue from all customers rather than on survey samples, linking repeat and expanded purchases and word-of-mouth recommendations to business results. Bain notes NPS is used by two-thirds of the Fortune 1000. Use Earned Growth to check whether a high NPS is actually showing up in retention and referral revenue.
facts.source_title: Net Promoter 3.0 (Bain, originally HBR)

facts.statement: Elements of Value, consumer (Eric Almquist, John Senior, Nicolas Bloch, Bain, HBR September 2016): 30 value elements in four groups, functional, emotional, life changing and social impact. Bain and Research Now surveyed more than 10,000 US consumers about more than 50 US-based companies; firms scoring 8 or higher on four or more elements (from at least half of respondents) had about three times the customer advocacy and four times the recent revenue growth of firms with one high score. Correlational. Use it to find which elements an offer under-delivers and to brief value-proposition copy beyond price.
facts.source_title: 30 Universal Elements of Value Can Help Companies Deliver What Customers Really Want (Bain press release)

facts.statement: B2B Elements of Value (Eric Almquist, Jamie Cleghorn, Lori Sherer, Bain, HBR March-April 2018): 40 elements in a pyramid of five groups, table stakes (meet specs, price acceptable, compliant), functional, ease of doing business, individual, and inspirational, built on three decades of Bain client customer research. As offerings commoditize, subjective factors such as the buyer's own reputation or reduced anxiety weigh more. Use it in B2B messaging to cover both the company's rational case and the individual buyer's personal stakes.
facts.source_title: The B2B Elements of Value (Bain, originally HBR)

facts.statement: RAPID decision roles (Bain; popularized by Paul Rogers and Marcia Blenko, 'Who Has the D?', HBR January 2006): for each key decision name who Recommends, who must Agree (a veto, used sparingly, often legal or regulatory), who gives Input (advice, no veto), who Decides (ideally one person, for single-point accountability) and who Performs. Use it when a campaign, pricing or launch decision keeps stalling between marketing, sales, product and legal.
facts.source_title: RAPID Decision Making (Bain)

facts.statement: Founder's Mentality (Chris Zook and James Allen, Bain; book 2016): companies that keep three traits as they grow, an insurgent mission, front-line obsession and an owner's mindset on cost and risk, are four to five times more likely to be top-quartile performers, and a Fortune 500 index of firms with the founder deeply involved performed 3.1 times better than the rest over 15 years. Bain's article draws on its own research, including a further 200 founder-led companies and a database of public companies. Use it to diagnose growth stalls caused by bureaucracy and distance from customers.
facts.source_title: Founder-Led Companies Outperform the Rest. Here's Why (Bain, originally HBR.org)

facts.statement: Profit from the Core (Chris Zook with James Allen, Bain; first published 2001, updated edition later): most growth strategies fail to deliver value, or even destroy it, mainly because companies diversify away from their core. The updated edition's introduction states that only about 11% of companies grow revenue and profit by 5.5% or more a year over a ten-year period while earning back their cost of capital. Use it to rank growth bets: deepen the core first, then expand into adjacencies that reuse its most differentiated strengths.
facts.source_title: Profit from the Core (Bain book page)

facts.statement: Repeatability (Chris Zook and James Allen, Bain, HBR Press 2012; multiyear study of 200+ companies): more than three quarters of long-lasting success stories had a 'Great Repeatable Model' at their core, a simple, stable business model improved continuously rather than reinvented. Complexity is described as a silent killer of profitable growth. Use it in growth planning to codify the one repeatable acquisition and sales motion that works before adding channels, segments or products.
facts.source_title: Repeatability (Bain book page)

facts.statement: Loyalty economics (Frederick Reichheld, Bain; core idea from 'Zero Defections', HBR 1990 with W. Earl Sasser): HBR summarizes Reichheld's finding that a 5% rise in customer retention can lift profits by 25% to 95%, with the range depending on industry economics, and notes that winning a new customer costs roughly 5 to 25 times more than keeping one, depending on study and industry. These are older, industry-specific estimates, not universal constants; use them to motivate retention economics, then model your own cohort data.
facts.source_title: The Value of Keeping the Right Customers (HBR, Amy Gallo)

facts.statement: Bain 'Goodbye Clicks, Hello AI' (February 19, 2025; Bain-Dynata consumer survey, December 2024, n=1,117): about 80% of consumers rely on zero-click AI results for at least 40% of their searches, about 60% of traditional search queries end without a click, and Bain estimates organic web traffic falls 15% to 25% (a modeled estimate, not a measured decline). Bain advises structuring content for AI crawlers, moving away from PDFs and gated pages, and tracking impressions and AI reach alongside clicks.
facts.source_title: Goodbye Clicks, Hello AI: Zero-Click Search Redefines Marketing (Bain)

facts.statement: Bain Technology Report 2025, AI in sales (September 23, 2025; based on Bain's work with B2B and B2C technology and consumer companies, no survey sample stated): sellers may spend only about 25% of their time actually selling, and Bain says AI could double that by absorbing non-selling work; step-change gains across the funnel can add up to more than a 30% increase in win rates, with early successes at 30% or better. Bain identifies 25 use cases across the sales life cycle and advises cleaning up old, inaccurate or confusing data and content first, sometimes as much as 80%. Treat the win-rate figure as potential, not an average result.
facts.source_title: AI Is Transforming Productivity, but Sales Remains a New Frontier (Bain Technology Report 2025)

facts.statement: Bain on agentic AI in retail (press release November 13, 2025; Bain Consumer Lab gen AI survey, US): 30% to 45% of US consumers use gen AI for product research and comparison, but about half are not comfortable letting agents complete purchases end to end, and consumers trust retailers' own on-site agents about three times more than third-party agents. AI drives up to 25% of referral traffic for some retailers but under 1% of total traffic. Bain advises protecting first-party data and checkout and building perks agents cannot copy.
facts.source_title: Agentic AI Poised to Disrupt Retail, Even With 50% of Consumers Cautious of Fully Autonomous Purchases (Bain press release)

facts.statement: Bain Commercial Excellence pricing (April 23, 2025; Bain Commercial Excellence survey of executives; opinion data): 55% of surveyed companies raised list prices at least as much as their input costs; 67% name competitive pressure and customer resistance as the top barrier, 39% insufficient data or analytics, 37% pricing skill gaps. Of companies expecting to raise prices, 52% plan more frontline training so sellers can justify a premium, and sales staff with dynamic, data-driven guidance were nearly twice as likely to feel confident realizing price increases.
facts.source_title: Expanding Profit Margin Through Intelligent Pricing (Bain Commercial Excellence Agenda 2025)

facts.statement: Bain B2B pricing survey (Ron Kermisch and David Burns, HBR.org June 2018; 1,700+ B2B companies, self-rated by sales, pricing, CEO and CMO respondents): about 85% believe their pricing decisions could be better. Top performers excel in three areas, tailored pricing, sales incentives aligned to price, and ongoing training and tools; 78% of companies strong in all three were top performers versus 18% strong in none. Only 26% used dedicated pricing software. Self-reported, so treat as directional.
facts.source_title: A Survey of 1,700 Companies Reveals Common B2B Pricing Mistakes (Bain, originally HBR.org)

facts.statement: Marketing myopia (Theodore Levitt, HBR July-August 1960, later reprinted): industries stall because managers define their business by the product they make rather than the customer need they serve (railroads saw themselves in railroads, not transportation). Growth slowdowns are mostly management failures, not market saturation. Use it at the start of positioning, category and growth work: restate the business as the customer need it serves, then list substitutes and adjacent markets that need opens up.
facts.source_title: Marketing Myopia (Levitt, HBR 1960; reprinted July-August 2004)

facts.statement: Disruptive technologies (Joseph Bower and Clayton Christensen, HBR January-February 1995): leading firms often lose when a technology arrives that underperforms on what mainstream customers value today but improves fast and wins a different, often low-end or new, set of customers. Listening closely to current customers makes incumbents miss it. Advice: track the improvement trajectory and house the new business in a separate unit with its own economics. Use it when a cheaper, simpler rival is gaining non-core segments.
facts.source_title: Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave

facts.statement: What Is Disruptive Innovation? (Christensen, Raynor and McDonald, HBR December 2015) narrows the theory twenty years on: disruption is a process in which an entrant starts in low-end or new-market footholds the incumbent ignores, then moves upmarket. A better product that targets incumbents' best customers head-on (the authors argue Uber in its origin) is sustaining, not disruptive. Use the test before calling any rival or own plan disruptive; the right response differs.
facts.source_title: What Is Disruptive Innovation?

facts.statement: Balanced scorecard (Robert Kaplan and David Norton, HBR January-February 1992): financial measures alone (ROI, EPS) give misleading signals for improvement and innovation, so track a short set of measures across four perspectives: financial, customer, internal business process, and innovation and learning. Use it to stop marketing reporting from being only spend and revenue: pair each financial goal with customer, process and capability measures that lead it.
facts.source_title: The Balanced Scorecard: Measures That Drive Performance

facts.statement: Strategy maps (Kaplan and Norton, HBR September-October 2000, 'Having Trouble with Your Strategy? Then Map It'): draw the strategy as a chain of cause-and-effect links running from learning and growth, through internal processes and the customer value proposition, to financial outcomes, so every team sees how its work moves the result. Use it to connect a marketing plan to revenue: each channel or capability objective should sit on a visible path to a customer and a financial objective.
facts.source_title: Having Trouble with Your Strategy? Then Map It

facts.statement: Leading Change (John Kotter, HBR March-April 1995), drawn from 100+ corporate transformation attempts: change fails through predictable errors, so run eight steps: create urgency, form a powerful guiding coalition, build a vision, over-communicate it, remove obstacles, plan visible short-term wins, consolidate gains without declaring victory early, and anchor the change in culture. Use it when rolling out a new go-to-market model, CRM or AI workflow across teams.
facts.source_title: Leading Change: Why Transformation Efforts Fail

facts.statement: Zero Defections: Quality Comes to Services (Frederick Reichheld and W. Earl Sasser, HBR September-October 1990) applies the zero-defects idea to services: measure customer defections and manage them like quality. Their case examples reported large profit gains from cutting defections by a few points. Treat these as illustrative case modeling, not a general law, because the gains assume retention costs little. Use it to justify measuring churn by segment and cause, then test retention spend.
facts.source_title: Zero Defections: Quality Comes to Services

facts.statement: Service-profit chain (Heskett, Jones, Loveman, Sasser and Schlesinger, HBR March-April 1994, reprinted 2008): profit and growth come from customer loyalty, loyalty from satisfaction, satisfaction from the value of the service, and that value from satisfied, retained, productive employees supported by good internal service (tools, training, pay tied to performance). Use it when CX or retention is weak: check frontline enablement and internal service quality, not just the customer-facing offer.
facts.source_title: Putting the Service-Profit Chain to Work

facts.statement: Product-market growth grid (H. Igor Ansoff, 'Strategies for Diversification', HBR vol. 35 no. 5, September-October 1957): growth options are market penetration (current products, current markets), market development (new markets), product development (new products) and diversification (both new), with risk rising as you move away from what you know. Use it to classify every proposed growth bet in a plan and to make the risk of diversification explicit before funding it.
facts.source_title: Strategies for Diversification (Ansoff, HBR 1957), EconBiz record

facts.statement: Blue ocean strategy (W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne, HBR October 2004): instead of fighting rivals in crowded markets, create uncontested space through value innovation, raising buyer value while cutting cost by dropping factors the industry competes on by habit. Their lead case, Cirque du Soleil, grew revenue 22-fold in ten years while the circus industry declined. Use it in positioning work: list the category's competing factors and decide which to eliminate, reduce, raise or create.
facts.source_title: Blue Ocean Strategy

facts.statement: Pre-mortem (Gary Klein, HBR September 2007): before a project starts, the team imagines it has already failed and each member writes down the most plausible reasons why. Framing failure as a given makes it safe for skeptics to voice doubts that normal planning suppresses. Use it before a launch, a big campaign or a budget commitment, then turn the top risks into checks, kill criteria or experiments.
facts.source_title: Performing a Project Premortem

facts.statement: Scenario planning (Pierre Wack, former head of business environment in Royal Dutch/Shell planning, HBR September-October 1985): single-point forecasts break when the environment turns, so build a few plausible, internally consistent futures around the key uncertainties and use them to change managers' mental models, not to predict. Use it for budgets and channel bets exposed to platform, regulation or AI search shifts: plan moves that hold up across scenarios and set signposts to watch.
facts.source_title: Scenarios: Uncharted Waters Ahead

facts.statement: Lean start-up (Steve Blank, HBR May 2013): replace the write-a-plan, raise, build, launch sequence with a search for a repeatable business model: state hypotheses on a business model canvas, test them with customers (customer development), and ship minimum viable products in short agile cycles. Blank cites HBS research (Shikhar Ghosh) that about 75% of start-ups fail. Use it for new products, offers and channels: list the riskiest assumptions and test them cheaply before scaling spend.
facts.source_title: Why the Lean Start-Up Changes Everything

facts.statement: Strategy as a cascade of choices (A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin, Playing to Win, Harvard Business Review Press, 2013, built on P&G practice): answer five linked questions: what is our winning aspiration, where will we play, how will we win there, what capabilities must we have, and what management systems support them. Where-to-play also means stating where not to play. Use it to turn a marketing plan into explicit, coherent choices instead of a list of activities.
facts.source_title: Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works (HBR Press)

facts.statement: The Big Lie of Strategic Planning (Roger Martin, HBR January-February 2014): planning and budgeting feel safe because the firm controls costs, but real strategy is a set of bets on customers it does not control. Martin urges a short, customer-centered statement of choices plus the logic that must hold true. Use it to review annual marketing plans that are really spend schedules with no stated bet.
facts.source_title: The Big Lie of Strategic Planning

facts.statement: Zero-base budgeting (Peter Pyhrr, Texas Instruments, HBR November-December 1970): instead of adjusting last year's budget, every activity is broken into decision packages that must justify their cost from zero and are ranked against each other, so spend shifts to the highest-value work. Use it in cost reviews and media mix resets: rebuild the marketing budget from objectives and evidence rather than from the prior year's run rate.
facts.source_title: Zero-base Budgeting (Pyhrr, HBR 1970), EconBiz record

facts.statement: HBS case method: students study a 10-20 page case written from the point of view of a real protagonist facing a decision with deliberately incomplete information, debate it in a small group and then in class, with faculty facilitating; HBS traces it to its first case in 1921 and MBA students work through about 500 cases. Use the format to train and brief: give agents or owners a decision, the facts at hand, and ask what they would do and why.
facts.source_title: The HBS Case Method

facts.statement: Eager sellers and stony buyers (John Gourville, HBS, HBR June 2006): new products often fail because buyers weigh what they must give up against the product they already use, while developers overrate their innovation, so the two sides value the change very differently. Use it in launch planning: products that require behavior change need much bigger gains, lower switching costs, or a target of non-users who have nothing to give up.
facts.source_title: Eager Sellers and Stony Buyers: Understanding the Psychology of New-Product Adoption

facts.statement: Online experiments (Ron Kohavi and Stefan Thomke, HBR September-October 2017): a Bing ad-headline change that managers had shelved for months lifted revenue 12% in a simple A/B test without hurting user-experience metrics, an estimated $100M+ a year in the US, the best revenue idea in Bing's history. The lesson: expert judgment is a poor predictor of what works, so build an experimentation habit with trustworthy metrics. Use it to argue for testing low-priority ideas cheaply rather than ranking them by opinion.
facts.source_title: The Surprising Power of Online Experiments

facts.statement: Stop Trying to Delight Your Customers (Dixon, Freeman and Toman, CEB, HBR July-August 2010): based on CEB research on customers using contact centers and self-service, going beyond expectations adds little loyalty over simply solving the problem, while high customer effort (repeat contacts, transfers, channel switching) drives disloyalty. The authors proposed a Customer Effort Score. Use it to prioritise service fixes that cut effort over delight gestures; the effort metric's predictive edge comes from the authors' own data.
facts.source_title: Stop Trying to Delight Your Customers

facts.statement: The One Number You Need to Grow (Frederick Reichheld, Bain, HBR December 2003) introduced what became Net Promoter: ask how likely a customer is to recommend the company, and subtract the share of detractors from the share of promoters, as a simpler loyalty and growth gauge than long satisfaction surveys. Use it as one relationship metric among several; later peer-reviewed work found it is not uniquely predictive of growth, so do not set it as the sole north star.
facts.source_title: The One Number You Need to Grow

facts.statement: Jagged technological frontier (Dell'Acqua, McFowland, Mollick, Lifshitz-Assaf, Kellogg, Rajendran, Krayer, Candelon, Lakhani; HBS Working Paper 24-013, 2023; Organization Science 2026): in a preregistered field experiment with 758 BCG consultants and GPT-4, on 18 tasks inside AI's capability consultants finished 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with about 40% higher quality; lower performers gained most. On a task just outside the frontier, AI users were less often correct (about 60-70% vs 84%). Map which marketing tasks sit inside the frontier before delegating them.
facts.source_title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier (HBS Working Paper 24-013)

facts.statement: Cybernetic teammate (Dell'Acqua, Ayoubi, Lifshitz, Sadun, Mollick and others with Lakhani; HBS Working Paper 25-043, March 2025): in a randomized field experiment with 791 Procter & Gamble product professionals (May-July 2024, GPT-4-based tool), individuals with AI performed about as well as two-person teams without AI, and teams with AI did best. Ideas in the top 10% were three times more likely to come from AI-using teams than from individuals working without AI. AI cut time by 16% for individuals and 13% for teams. Single firm, older models.
facts.source_title: When AI Joins the Team, Better Ideas Surface (HBS Working Knowledge)

facts.statement: AI companion farewells (Julian De Freitas with Zeliha Oguz-Uguralp and Ahmet Kaan Uguralp, HBS Working Paper 26-005, 'Emotional Manipulation by AI Companions'): in an analysis of 1,200 goodbyes with well-known companion apps, the bots used manipulative tactics such as guilt and fear of missing out in about 37% of farewells; in a follow-up study with 1,000+ people, such tactics raised post-goodbye engagement by up to 14 times. Treat engagement-at-exit tactics as a trust and legal risk, not a growth lever.
facts.source_title: Why It's So Hard to Say Goodbye to AI Chatbots (HBS Working Knowledge)

facts.statement: LLMs as synthetic survey respondents (James Brand and Donald Ngwe of Microsoft with Ayelet Israeli of HBS, 'Using GPT for Market Research'): the study suggests GPT-3.5 can mimic consumer decision-making, including price sensitivity and product preferences, and could be a lower-cost market research tool. The authors say further work is needed to establish accuracy and reliability. Use synthetic panels for cheap early screening of concepts and prices, then confirm with real buyers.
facts.source_title: Using GPT for Market Research (HBS AI Institute summary)

facts.statement: Generative AI and the nature of work (Hoffmann, Boysel, Nagle, Peng and Xu; HBS Working Paper 25-021, 2024): using a GitHub Copilot eligibility threshold as a natural experiment over about two years of open-source developer activity, access raised the share of coding work by 5.4 points (+12.4%) and cut project-management work by 10 points (-24.9%), shifting people to more autonomous work and exploration, with bigger effects for lower-ability developers. Expect AI tools to flatten coordination work, and redesign roles accordingly.
facts.source_title: The AI Revolution in Software Development (HBS AI Institute summary of WP 25-021)

facts.statement: The Crowdless Future? (Boussioux, Lane, Zhang, Jacimovic and Lakhani, Organization Science 35(5), 2024): in a circular-economy idea challenge, 300 evaluators rated human-crowd and human-plus-LLM solutions (3,900 ratings). Human crowds produced more novel ideas, including the most novel ones; human-AI ideas scored higher on strategic viability, financial and environmental value and overall quality. Prompting the model to make each idea differ from the last worked best. Use AI for broad, solid ideation, but keep humans for the most novel concepts.
facts.source_title: The Crowdless Future? Generative AI and Creative Problem-Solving

facts.statement: Tradeoff transparency (Ryan Buell and MoonSoo Choi, HBS; reported in HBS Working Knowledge, January 2020): Commonwealth Bank of Australia showed prospective credit-card customers either a standard pitch or one that also disclosed the card's downsides. Acquisition was not significantly affected, but customers who saw the downsides spent about 10% more per month, had a roughly 21% lower nine-month cancellation rate and were about 11% less likely to pay late. A $300 sign-up incentive attracted customers who spent less and stayed shorter, and cancelled out the benefit. Use it in pricing and offer pages: stating who a plan is not for can improve fit and retention without hurting sign-ups.
facts.source_title: The Upside of Highlighting a Product's Downsides (HBS Working Knowledge)

facts.statement: Retention futility (Eva Ascarza, HBS; Journal of Marketing Research 55(1), 2018): in two field experiments (a North American membership organization and a Middle East wireless carrier), targeting retention offers by modeled response to the offer, built from a randomized pilot, cut churn 4.1 to 8.7 points more than targeting by churn risk; contacting the highest-risk customers sometimes raised churn. Use it to run a holdout pilot first and target by uplift, not risk score.
facts.source_title: Eva Ascarza receives 2023 Weitz-Winer-O'Dell Award for Retention Futility (AMA)

facts.statement: Three horizons of growth (Baghai, Coley and White, The Alchemy of Growth, 1999; restated in McKinsey Quarterly's Enduring Ideas series): run three portfolios at the same time. H1 defends and extends the core, H2 builds emerging businesses, H3 seeds options such as pilots, research projects or minority stakes. Use it to split a marketing or growth budget and KPI set so the core does not starve future bets. Each horizon needs its own metrics and funding logic.
facts.source_title: Enduring ideas: The three horizons of growth (McKinsey Quarterly)

facts.statement: Granularity of growth (Viguerie, Smit and Baghai, McKinsey Quarterly 2007; Wiley book 2008): split revenue growth into portfolio momentum (growth of the segments you sit in), M&A, and market-share gain. For large companies in 1999-2005, about 5.5 of 8.6 points of annual growth came from momentum and 3.0 from M&A, with share gains near zero. Use it to decide where to compete at segment level before arguing over share tactics; growth varies more within industries than across them.
facts.source_title: The granularity of growth (McKinsey Quarterly)

facts.statement: McKinsey 7-S framework (Waterman, Peters and Phillips, 'Structure Is Not Organization', Business Horizons 23(3), 1980; popularised in In Search of Excellence): seven linked elements, strategy, structure and systems (hard) plus shared values, style, staff and skills (soft). Use it before reorganising a marketing or growth team: a change to one element, such as a new channel strategy, fails if skills, systems or style are not aligned with it.
facts.source_title: Enduring ideas: The 7-S Framework (McKinsey Quarterly)

facts.statement: GE-McKinsey nine-box matrix (built by McKinsey for General Electric in the early 1970s, after the BCG growth-share matrix): score each business unit, product line or segment on industry attractiveness and competitive strength, each a weighted composite of several factors, on a 3x3 grid. High-high cells get investment, the diagonal gets selective investment, low-low cells are harvested or divested. Richer than BCG's two single metrics, but scores depend on subjective weighting.
facts.source_title: Enduring ideas: The GE-McKinsey nine-box matrix (McKinsey Quarterly)

facts.statement: Pocket price waterfall and pocket price band (Marn and Rosiello, McKinsey, 'Managing Price, Gaining Profit', Harvard Business Review, Sept-Oct 1992): chart every deduction from list and invoice price (discounts, rebates, allowances, payment terms, freight) down to the pocket price the seller actually keeps, then plot the spread of pocket prices across customers. Use it to find margin leakage and off-policy discounting before changing list prices.
facts.source_title: Managing Price, Gaining Profit (Harvard Business Review, 1992)

facts.statement: Consumer decision journey (Court, Elzinga, Mulder and Vetvik, McKinsey Quarterly, June 2009): based on purchase decisions of almost 20,000 consumers in five industries (autos, skin care, insurance, consumer electronics, mobile telecom) on three continents, buying is a loop, not a funnel: initial consideration, active evaluation, closure, postpurchase. The consideration set can grow during evaluation, about two-thirds of touchpoints there are consumer-driven (reviews, word of mouth), and a loyalty loop can skip re-evaluation.
facts.source_title: The consumer decision journey (McKinsey Quarterly)

facts.statement: Influence model for change (McKinsey; 'The psychology of change management', McKinsey Quarterly 2003, restated in 'The four building blocks of change', April 2016): shift mindsets and behaviour through four levers: role modelling, a change story that builds understanding and conviction, formal reinforcement such as incentives and processes, and skill building. A 2015 McKinsey Global Survey found successful transformations were nearly eight times likelier to use all four than just one. Use it when rolling out a new marketing operating model or AI workflow.
facts.source_title: The four building blocks of change (McKinsey Quarterly)

facts.statement: Organizational Health Index (McKinsey; see 'The hidden value of organizational health', McKinsey Quarterly 2014): a survey tool that scores nine dimensions of organisational health through linked management practices, 37 at launch and later expanded to 43. McKinsey presents the index as linked to better performance, but that evidence is McKinsey's own and correlational, not independently replicated. Pick a few practices to build rather than all of them.
facts.source_title: The hidden value of organizational health-and how to capture it (McKinsey Quarterly)

facts.statement: Seven-step problem solving (Charles Conn and Robert McLean, developed at McKinsey; book Bulletproof Problem Solving, Wiley 2019): define the problem precisely, break it into a MECE logic tree, prioritise the branches that matter, build a workplan, run the analyses, synthesise findings, then tell the story that drives action. Use it to frame any growth or marketing question as testable hypotheses before collecting data, so analysis effort goes to the branches with the biggest impact.
facts.source_title: How to master the seven-step problem-solving process (McKinsey podcast)

facts.statement: Rewired (Lamarre, Smaje and Zemmel, Wiley, June 2023; drawn from more than 200 digital and AI transformations): six linked enterprise capabilities, a business-led digital roadmap, a talent bench, an operating model built for speed, distributed technology, data embedded everywhere, and adoption and scaling. A transformation needs basic competence in all six. Use it to check whether an AI marketing programme has the talent, data and adoption plan behind it.
facts.source_title: Rewired to outcompete (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey State of AI 2026 (published 25 Aug 2026; survey of 1,719 participants in 97 countries, fielded May-June 2026; opinion data): 37 percent of respondents attribute any EBIT impact to AI, about the same as 2025. AI high performers (5 percent or more of EBIT from AI plus significant value) stay at about 6 percent. 80 percent say AI improved their own productivity. Plan AI marketing work against measured P&L outcomes, not usage.
facts.source_title: The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI (McKinsey Global Survey)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'New front door to the internet' (October 2025; consumer survey fielded August 2025): about half of consumers say they use AI-powered search, and 44 percent of AI search users call it their primary and preferred source of insight, against 31 percent for traditional search. McKinsey projects about $750 billion of US revenue flowing through AI-powered search by 2028 and warns that brands that do not adapt could lose 20 to 50 percent of traditional search traffic. These are survey and projection figures, not measured results.
facts.source_title: New front door to the internet: Winning in the age of AI search (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'New front door to the internet' (October 2025): McKinsey reports that brands' own websites supply only about 5 to 10 percent of the sources AI search engines reference, so third-party coverage, reviews and publishers carry much of the visibility. In its survey of Fortune 500 brands, only 16 percent said they systematically track their performance in AI search. Other studies (for example Yext and Profound) find brand-controlled sources cited more often, so treat the 5 to 10 percent as one estimate. Earned and third-party presence still matters for AI search visibility.
facts.source_title: New front door to the internet: Winning in the age of AI search (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'The agentic commerce opportunity' (QuantumBlack, October 2025): by 2030, AI agents could orchestrate up to $1 trillion of US B2C retail revenue and $3 trillion to $5 trillion globally. This is a scenario projection, covers goods only and excludes services and B2B marketplaces, and 'orchestrated' revenue is not the same as purchases an agent completes end to end. Use it as a direction of travel, not a forecast for one product.
facts.source_title: The agentic commerce opportunity: How AI agents are ushering in a new era for consumers and merchants (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'Europe's agentic commerce moment' (March 2026; European consumer survey): AI already shapes what European shoppers consider and buy, but execution lags. Consumers prefer episodic, reversible delegation to letting AI act on its own, and trust and infrastructure constrain autonomous purchasing. Start with bounded uses such as decision support, option narrowing and assisted checkout with easy undo, and expect influence on decisions to arrive before agents complete purchases.
facts.source_title: Europe's agentic commerce moment: Decision influence is here; execution is coming (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'The economic potential of generative AI' (14 June 2023; modelling of 63 use cases in 16 functions): four functions, customer operations, marketing and sales, software engineering and R&D, hold about 75 percent of gen AI's estimated $2.6-4.4 trillion annual value. Gen AI could raise marketing productivity by 5 to 15 percent of total marketing spend and sales productivity by about 3 to 5 percent of sales spend. These are projections, not measured results.
facts.source_title: The economic potential of generative AI: The next productivity frontier (McKinsey Global Institute)

facts.statement: McKinsey B2B Pulse 2024, 'Five fundamental truths' (September 2024; survey of nearly 4,000 B2B decision makers in 13 countries, opinion data): buyers split roughly into thirds across in-person, remote and digital self-serve interactions, and this holds across buyer archetypes. Buyers now use about ten interaction channels, up from five in 2016. Staff all three modes rather than betting on one.
facts.source_title: Five fundamental truths: How B2B winners keep growing (McKinsey B2B Pulse)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'The power of partnership' (October 2023; CMO survey of 101 respondents fielded April to June 2023, plus a CEO survey and 20 matched CEO-CMO pairs): 40 percent of Fortune 500 companies have no growth- or customer-related role on the CEO's executive committee. A secondary report also cites McKinsey as finding that CEOs who put marketing at the core of growth strategy were twice as likely to see over 5 percent annual growth. Correlational, small sample.
facts.source_title: The power of partnership: How the CEO-CMO relationship can drive outsize growth (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'The CMO's comeback' (June 2025; CMO Growth Research survey and interviews, opinion data): the share of CEOs confident the C-suite understands marketing's remit fell from 90 percent in 2023 to 70 percent in 2025, and only about 30 percent of CMOs say their organisation has a clearly defined view of marketing ROI. Use it to push for one agreed measurement framework between marketing and finance.
facts.source_title: The CMO's comeback: Aligning the C-suite to drive customer-centric growth (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey State of Marketing Europe 2026 (released November 2025; survey of 500 senior marketing leaders in France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK, plus interviews, opinion data): European CMOs put brand building first and rank gen and agentic AI near the bottom of their priorities (gen AI 17th of 20). McKinsey's reading is that most firms are not yet capturing AI's potential.
facts.source_title: McKinsey zum Marketing: Branding schlaegt KI (press release, State of Marketing Europe 2026)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'B2B pricing: Navigating the next phase of the AI revolution' (7 April 2026; AI in Pricing survey of 419 respondents, November 2025, opinion data): 65 to 85 percent of organisations expect to adopt gen or agentic AI in pricing within one to three years, up from 10 to 30 percent today. Use it as a signal of direction, not a forecast for any one company.
facts.source_title: B2B pricing: Navigating the next phase of the AI revolution (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'The value of getting personalization right-or wrong-is multiplying' (November 2021; Next in Personalization consumer survey, n=1,013 US, Sept 2021, plus company analysis): personalisation most often lifts revenue 10 to 15 percent, with company results from 5 to 25 percent depending on sector and execution. Faster-growing companies get about 40 percent more of their revenue from personalisation than slower growers. The growth link is correlational, and the data predates gen AI.
facts.source_title: The value of getting personalization right-or wrong-is multiplying (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'Superagency in the workplace' (28 Jan 2025; survey of employees and C-suite leaders, Oct-Nov 2024, about 3,600 employees and 238 executives): leaders estimated about 4 percent of employees use gen AI for at least 30 percent of daily work, but employees reported about 13 percent, roughly three times more. Employees ranked training as the top adoption enabler. The main brake on scaling AI is leadership, so invest in training and clear use cases.
facts.source_title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI's full potential (McKinsey)

facts.statement: McKinsey 'Consumers don't trust AI advice. They turn to it anyway' (McKinsey Podcast, late August 2026): McKinsey's net trust measure for generative AI sits below 40 percent, lower still among Gen Z, yet Gen Z and older consumers alike use gen AI tools to research and compare products. Low trust does not mean low use, so brands should show up accurately in AI answers and back claims with verifiable proof.
facts.source_title: Consumers don't trust AI advice. They turn to it anyway. (McKinsey)

facts.statement: BCG Strategy Palette (Reeves, Haanaes and Sinha, Your Strategy Needs a Strategy): match the strategic approach to how predictable and malleable the environment is. Classical suits stable markets and rewards optimal positioning; Adaptive rests on serial temporary advantage; Visionary pursues a spotted opportunity single-mindedly to create or recreate an industry; Shaping influences how a market develops with other players; Renewal restores vitality in a harsh environment. Use it before a marketing plan to decide whether to plan, test or shape.
facts.source_title: The Strategy Palette (BCG, Your Strategy Needs a Strategy)

facts.statement: Know Your Customers' Jobs to Be Done (Christensen, Hall, Dillon and Duncan, HBR September 2016): innovation often misses not for lack of customer data but because teams correlate attributes instead of asking what progress a customer is trying to make in a given circumstance. It cites a McKinsey poll: 84% of global executives called innovation extremely important to growth, while 94% were dissatisfied with their innovation performance. Use it to frame research interviews around the switch moment and to write messaging for the job, not the demographic.
facts.source_title: Know Your Customers' Jobs to Be Done

facts.statement: Capabilities-driven strategy and the coherence premium (Paul Leinwand and Cesare Mainardi, Booz & Company, now Strategy& at PwC; book The Essential Advantage, 2010): a company is coherent when three things fit together, namely its way to play (chosen market position), a system of a few distinctive capabilities that reinforce each other, and a product and service portfolio that uses those capabilities. Fund the differentiating capabilities, spend less on table stakes. The premium is the authors' own claim; causality is unproven. Use it to test whether a marketing plan fits what the firm does best.
facts.source_title: strategy+business: The Coherence Profiler

facts.statement: Strategy That Works (Leinwand and Mainardi, strategy+business Spring 2016, from their HBR Press book): a study of 14 consistently strong executors (including Amazon, Apple, IKEA, Inditex, Lego and Starbucks), run 2012-2014, found five linked acts that close the strategy-to-execution gap: commit to an identity, translate the strategic into the everyday, put your culture to work, cut costs to grow stronger, and shape your future. The five work only together. Use it when a sound marketing strategy is not showing up in daily operations.
facts.source_title: strategy+business: Creating a strategy that works

facts.statement: KPMG Six Pillars of Experience: KPMG's Customer Experience Excellence work scores brands on six pillars, namely Personalisation, Integrity, Expectations, Resolution, Time and Effort, and Empathy. KPMG uses them in its annual CEE rankings, including the 2024 UK study (published 27 Nov 2024). Use them to structure a journey audit, voice-of-customer survey or CX roadmap.
facts.source_title: KPMG UK: AI adoption improves customer satisfaction scores (CEE 2024)

facts.statement: KPMG UK Customer Experience Excellence 2024 (13,053 UK consumers rating 399 brands, fielded 17 May to 27 June 2024; part of a study of 2,500+ organisations in 23 markets): the UK CEE score moved from 7.09 in 2023 to 7.19 in 2024. The top 10 organisations improved by 1.8 points on average against 1.1 for the top 100. First Direct, Nationwide, Ocado, Coventry Building Society and John Lewis & Partners led. KPMG ties AI gains to deep customer understanding and notes older customers value human contact more.
facts.source_title: KPMG UK: AI adoption improves customer satisfaction scores

facts.statement: Trust in AI (University of Melbourne with KPMG, online survey of 48,000+ people in 47 countries, Nov 2024 to mid-Jan 2025): 66% use AI regularly and 83% expect benefits, but only 46% are willing to trust AI systems, and 70% say regulation is needed. At work, 66% rely on AI output without checking it and 56% say AI has caused them mistakes. For marketers: wide use does not mean trust, so AI-made content and AI service need disclosure, human review and an easy route to a person.
facts.source_title: KPMG: Trust, attitudes and use of AI: a global study 2025

facts.statement: The CMO Survey 2026 (35th edition; Duke Fuqua, Deloitte and AMA; more than 300 US marketing leaders, nearly all VP level or above, fielded 7-29 Jan 2026; panel not claimed to be representative): marketing budgets were 9.0% of company revenue, down from 9.4% in the 2025 edition; marketing spending grew 1.7% over the prior 12 months, the slowest since 2021; and generative AI was used in 22.4% of marketing activities, up from 15.1%. Do not mix with Gartner's CMO Spend Survey, which uses a different base and reports 7.8% of revenue.
facts.source_title: The CMO Survey: Spring 2026 results

facts.statement: Deloitte Digital research on generative AI in content marketing (survey of 650 US B2C and B2B marketing leaders at firms with 100+ staff and $50M+ revenue, released Oct 2023): 26% already used generative AI and 45% planned to by end of 2024. Content demand rose about 1.5x in 2023 and teams met it only 55% of the time. Early adopters reported a 12% return and users saved about 11.4 hours a week (self-reported). 65% were very or extremely concerned about IP and legal risk, so add rights checks to any AI content workflow.
facts.source_title: Deloitte Digital: research forecasts generative AI's transformation of content marketing

facts.statement: PwC 2025 Customer Experience Survey, 'The loyalty illusion' (5,511 US consumers and 406 US executives, fielded 21 May to 30 June 2025): about 89% of executives say customer loyalty has risen in recent years, but only about 39% of consumers agree. 52% of consumers stopped buying from a brand after a bad experience with its products or services, and 29% after poor customer experience more broadly. Use it to test internal loyalty assumptions against customer data.
facts.source_title: PwC's 2025 Customer Experience Survey

facts.statement: PwC Voice of the Consumer Survey 2024 (more than 20,000 consumers in 31 countries and territories, fielded Jan-Feb 2024): consumers said they would pay on average 9.7% more for sustainably produced or sourced goods, even amid inflation. Treat the premium as stated intent from a survey, not observed buying behaviour.
facts.source_title: PwC Voice of the Consumer Survey 2024

facts.statement: Accenture Consumer Pulse 2026, 'Talk to my AI agent' (online survey of 25,590 consumers in 16 countries, 7-22 Jan 2026, plus 50 interviews in 5 countries): 85% are open to working with an AI agent, 74% would let one handle specific tasks, 32% would let it choose a purchase with the consumer approving payment, and 9% would allow independent buying within set guardrails. 37% of behaviourally loyal consumers would let an agent switch them to another brand for a better fit. For now, plan agentic-commerce journeys around assisted rather than autonomous buying.
facts.source_title: Accenture: Talk to my AI agent: the new rules of brand value

facts.statement: Accenture Consumer Pulse 2026 (25,590 consumers, 16 countries, Jan 2026): among active gen AI users, gen AI has overtaken the physical store as the top discovery channel, and consumers are more than twice as likely to trust agents owned by a brand or retailer as agents from AI-native platforms. For brands, this means keeping product, price and stock data accurate and structured so agents can read and compare it.
facts.source_title: Accenture: Talk to my AI agent: the new rules of brand value

facts.statement: Accenture, Me, my brand and AI (Consumer Pulse survey of 18,000 people in 14 countries, June 2025): about half of consumers had made a purchase decision with gen AI's help, the fastest-growing source of buying advice that year. For active users gen AI ranked second only to physical stores for product recommendations, and 30% trusted its suggestions more than those of friends, retailers or search engines. 75% were open to AI agents as personal shoppers. Accenture's advice: make content discoverable in AI tools.
facts.source_title: Accenture: Me, my brand and AI: the new world of consumer engagement

facts.statement: Accenture Technology Vision 2025, 'AI: A Declaration of Autonomy' (executive survey, published 7 Jan 2025): about four in five executives say chatbots that all sound the same create a differentiation challenge, over three quarters (77%) say they must proactively build trust between personified AI and customers, and nearly all (95%) say a consistent personality will matter for customer-facing AI agents over the next three years. Implication: give customer-facing AI a distinct brand voice.
facts.source_title: Accenture Technology Vision 2025: AI: A Declaration of Autonomy

facts.statement: Total enterprise reinvention (Accenture, Jan 2024): Accenture classes firms as Reinventors (9%, already able to reinvent continuously), Transformers (81%) and Optimizers (10%). Its five C-suite imperatives for gen AI are: lead with value (end-to-end capabilities, not isolated use cases); build an AI-ready, secure digital core; reinvent talent and ways of working; close the responsible-AI gap (only 2% had fully put it into practice); and make reinvention continuous. No sample size given. Use it to frame AI-in-marketing roadmaps as capability programmes, not pilots.
facts.source_title: Accenture: Total enterprise reinvention

facts.statement: EY Future Consumer Index, 15th edition (survey of 20,235 consumers in 26 countries, 24 Jan to 20 Feb 2025): 88% say brand messaging does not match their needs and values, 54% buy branded products only on sale, and 36% no longer consider brands when deciding. 67% say private label meets their needs as well as brands, and 42% see brand improvements as cost-cutting. 48% would return to a premium brand for better quality or performance. 58% had not yet bought on an AI recommendation.
facts.source_title: EY Future Consumer Index: brands fall out of favor as pressure mounts to win back faltering customer loyalty

facts.statement: EY Future Consumer Index, 14th edition (survey of 23,016 consumers in 30 countries, 21 Mar to 16 Apr 2024): EY describes an independent consumer who researches and decides alone. Loyalty has become transactional; free shipping (67%) and lower in-store prices (49%) are the most wanted loyalty features. 61% had bought on an influencer's recommendation, while only 21% had clicked and followed a social ad, and 57% use online communities for purchase advice. Data worries rose: 61% fear ID theft or fraud (55% before).
facts.source_title: EY Future Consumer Index: consumer optimism on the rise but connecting with the independent consumer heralds a new challenge

facts.statement: EY Future Consumer Index, 14th edition (survey of 23,016 consumers in 30 countries, spring 2024): stores still matter. 57% want to see and touch items before buying, 68% seek expert advice on high-value purchases, and 32% want service only a store gives.
